posts.title: Hawaii Home Grow Rules, Plainly
posts.subtitle: What Hawaii's statutes, its health department's rules and its 2025 laws say about growing medical cannabis at home, laid out in the order a grower meets them.
posts.description: Hawaii's plant limit, grow site, tag, caregiver, travel and driving rules for medical cannabis, read from the statutes, the 2025 acts and OMCCR's own documents.

r: Educational information, not legal advice. Education, not medical advice. This piece reads public texts. It cannot tell you how a law applies to your home, your card or your neighbors.

A Hawaii patient who grows medical cannabis at home is following three layers of text at once. The first is a statute, part IX of chapter 329 of the Hawaii Revised Statutes. The second is an administrative rule, chapter 11-160 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules. The third is guidance from the Department of Health's Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation, known as OMCCR: web pages, a flyer, a newsletter and a public workshop deck. The layers do not always use the same words, and 2025 changed the statute. This piece lines them up and says which layer each sentence comes from.

I read the statute sections, both 2025 session laws, the rules OMCCR posts and OMCCR's public pages and documents on October 11, 2026. The legislature's main website refused my automated request that day, so I read each statute section and both session laws on its data site, data.capitol.hawaii.gov. The statute listing there carries a compilation date of January 5, 2026, which includes the 2025 acts. I did not search the 2026 session laws. Where I describe what a section said before 2025, I take it from the session law's own marked-up text.

Section 329-130 lists the lawful sources of medical cannabis for a qualifying patient. As amended by Act 46 of 2025, a patient gets it from a licensed dispensary, by growing an adequate supply under section 329-122, or from the patient's primary caregiver, who grows an adequate supply for that patient.
OMCCR's Growing Cannabis page gives the same three growers: a dispensary, a primary caregiver and a qualifying patient.

The Legislature put numbers on why this matters. In the findings of Act 46, it cites a 2022 Department of Health rapid survey in which 55 percent of patients said they got their cannabis only from a licensed dispensary. The Act reads that to mean that up to 45 percent get it from other sources, including cultivation. It also says some patients cannot grow their own supply because of disability or lack of space, and that those patients should keep the option of having a caregiver grow for them.
The statute caps a patient's "adequate supply" at ten cannabis plants, whether immature or mature. The same definition sets a limit on usable cannabis, which I leave to the statute's text.
OMCCR's May 2024 newsletter adds a practical reading: the ten-plant limit covers plants at any stage, and a clone or an immature plant counts as one plant.

The limit is joint. The definition says the supply is "jointly possessed" by the patient and the caregiver, so a caregiver's plants and a patient's plants for the same patient share one ten-plant ceiling.

blocks.x: The grow site goes on the card

r: A patient who wants a grow site names it on the registration application. The department's rule defines a grow site as a specific location, identified by street address, tax map key number or a description that pins down the physical location, and says it must be the patient's or caregiver's residential address or another location the patient or caregiver owns or controls.
OMCCR's page says the same and adds that the site must appear on the 329 card.

The May 2024 newsletter says only one grow site can be designated, and that the patient swears "under perjury of law," in the newsletter's words, that the patient or caregiver lives at, owns or controls it.
The rule's application list asks for the same attestation.

The rule says the patient or caregiver designated to cultivate "shall have a legible identification tag, in a form and manner as determined by the department, on each cannabis plant being cultivated."

OMCCR fills in the form in a tagging flyer, last revised July 27, 2017. The tag shows the 329 registration number and the expiration date. It hangs from or around the bottom of the plant. It is made of durable, weather-resistant material in a solid color, with black or blue lettering, at least 3 inches by one quarter inch, and it must be easy to see from outside the plant. If the lettering gets hard to read, the tag must be replaced at once with the same number and date.

The flyer ties the tags to the card. Tags must be updated immediately when a new registration card is issued, including after a renewal or a change to the card that gives it a new registration number. It also says no more than ten plants at one registered location should carry the same registration number and expiration date.

The flyer also carries a warning. Untagged or improperly tagged plants "are subject to confiscation and removal by law enforcement," and the grower or property owner is not guaranteed the protections in chapter 329.
OMCCR's public Know Before You Grow deck from March 7, 2026 repeats the tag specifications on a slide.

OMCCR's page answers this one in a sentence. No one outside the registered patient and the one primary caregiver named on the card may handle the patient's plants or usable cannabis. The page lists the verbs: touch, water, harvest, take care of.

The May 2024 newsletter adds that a patient may not assign the right to grow, handle or process plants to a grow site or a third party, and that a grow site or cooperative cannot be a caregiver. Only a registered primary caregiver may help.

Caregivers are where the rules moved most. Before 2025, section 329-130 said that after December 31, 2024, no primary caregiver would be authorized to cultivate cannabis for a patient, with exceptions for a minor patient and for patients on an island with no licensed dispensary. Act 46 prints that language struck through.

In late December 2024, Governor Josh Green signed Executive Order 24-06. OMCCR's summary says the order acknowledges that caregivers had been allowed to grow up to ten plants because some patients cannot grow for themselves, and orders OMCCR to give low priority to minor violations of part IX, including a caregiver growing an adequate supply for one patient. The same summary says patients filing new or renewal applications would not be able to officially designate a caregiver to cultivate from January 1, 2025.

Act 46 changed the statute. The governor signed it on May 14, 2025. Its caregiver and sources provisions took effect retroactive to January 1, 2025. It deleted the sunset language in section 329-130 and added the caregiver as a lawful source. It also rewrote section 329-123(c) so that each primary caregiver is responsible for not more than five qualifying patients at a time, instead of one.

OMCCR's guidance sheet for caregivers says the same: caregivers may cultivate again, and each may be registered with no more than five patients. The sheet adds that a minor patient may register up to two caregivers if both are the minor's parent, guardian or legal custodian.
One thing did not change. Every qualifying patient has only one primary caregiver at any given time. That rule sits in section 329-123(b), and Act 46 did not touch it.
OMCCR's Growing page still says so.

blocks.x: How many patients can share a place

r: Here the texts use different words. The statute, in the new section 329-130, says each location used to cultivate cannabis shall be used for not more than five qualifying patients. It says this in two places, once for a patient growing and once for a caregiver growing.
An OMCCR newsletter from November 2024 had already described the same cap, citing section 329-130.
OMCCR's caregiver sheet says: "No single location shall be permitted to have more than five grow sites registered to it."

That counts grow sites. The statute counts patients. Because each patient names one grow site, the two likely line up, but the sheet does not say they are the same thing and I do not treat them as one.

OMCCR's public deck for its March 7, 2026 Know Before You Grow workshop turns the cap into plants. It says a single caregiver may now care for up to five qualifying patients, up to 50 plants may be grown on one registered grow site, up to ten per patient may be grown, and every plant must be marked with the 329 number and card expiration date.
That is OMCCR's reading in a deck. The statute does not state a fifty-plant total.

blocks.x: What breaking the rules can cost

r: Act 46 also added a new section to part IX, now codified as section 329-132. Anyone who violates the part or its rules can be fined up to $5,000 for each separate violation, and each day a violation occurs or continues counts as a separate offense. The department may impose the penalty administratively, with a written notice that can come with a cease and desist order or an order for corrective action. A person who disagrees has twenty calendar days to ask for a contested case hearing.

The Act says the fine is in addition to any other penalty the law allows. Section 329-125 lets a patient or caregiver raise medical use as an affirmative defense in a marijuana prosecution, but only if the person "strictly complied" with part IX. A person who goes outside the permitted scope does not get the protection against searches and seizures that the program otherwise offers.
The word to hold on to is strictly. The items a grower can check against the text are the tag, the site on the card, who handles the plants and how many patients share a location.

Section 329-122(e) lists where the authorization to use medical cannabis does not reach: a school bus, a public bus or any moving vehicle, a workplace, school grounds, a public park or beach, and any place open to the public. It then makes room for travel. A patient or caregiver may transport cannabis or a manufactured cannabis product in a public place if it is in a sealed container, not visible to the public, and not removed from the container or used while in the public place.
OMCCR's August 2024 newsletter summarizes the rule in the same terms: sealed container, not visible, not consumed in public.

Between islands, the statute is firm. For interisland transport, "transport" of cannabis by any means is allowed only between dispensaries, to the extent authorized by the dispensary law, and between a production center or retail location and a certified laboratory for testing. The section says state law and its protections do not apply outside the State, and that allowable transport does not include interisland transport between a patient or caregiver and anyone else.
The OMCCR newsletter says the same in one line: a patient may not transport medical cannabis interisland or to the continent.

A patient or caregiver who carries a sample to a certified laboratory needs an appointment and a confirmation, which may be electronic, ready during transport. The statute also limits the size of that sample, and I leave the figure to the text.
OMCCR's newsletter tells patients that a 329 card does not protect against a citation for driving under the influence or for operating a vehicle under the influence of an intoxicant, called OVUII.

The offense statute names drugs in general. It says a person commits the offense by operating or taking actual physical control of a vehicle "under the influence of any drug that impairs the person's ability to operate the vehicle in a careful and prudent manner."

The card appears nowhere in that sentence. The OMCCR flyer called Be a Good Neighbor says "Don't Drive" and adds that although medical cannabis is legal, driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal. It also says all use of medical cannabis must be on private property and that plants should be kept secure, out of the neighbors' view and out of reach of children.

OMCCR's pages say the Department of Health would roll out a new patient registry portal on September 30, 2026. The page describing it says patients must log in to the new portal starting September 30 to download their new 329 card, that patient and provider logins stay the same, and that the old site would be down for a stretch in late September.

The Patient Forms page lists video and PDF guides under "New Registry System Resources (Launching 9/30/2026)." One of them, a five-page guide, walks a patient through signing in and printing a digital card.

The pages still use the future tense, and the Registry home page still showed a blackout notice for applications when I read it, so the public pages do not let me confirm that the rollout happened on schedule. I also looked for a public statement that registration numbers changed with the new system. The pages I read do not say so. They say nothing about numbers either way. A grower with plants in the ground has one reliable check, and it is the flyer's: when a new card is issued, update the tags to match it.
Section 329D-24 says nothing in the dispensary chapter shall be construed as prohibiting a qualifying patient or primary caregiver from cultivating or possessing an adequate supply under part IX.

Then Act 241 of 2025, signed June 27, 2025, took effect July 1, 2025, except that its part IV takes effect January 1, 2028. Part IV adds a new section to the dispensary chapter. It begins: "Notwithstanding section 329D-24, it shall be unlawful for any person to cultivate cannabis without a license issued by the department pursuant to this section." It then lists what the new cannabis cultivator license allows, including distributing cannabis plants and flower to a medical cannabis dispensary. The text of the new section does not mention patients or caregivers.

I do not know how the two fit together. A reader could argue that the new section is about commercial cultivation, which OMCCR describes as a way to widen the variety of flower and products sold by dispensaries.

A reader could also point to the words "any person" and the reference to section 329D-24. The Department's public pages that I read say nothing on the point, and OMCCR's March 2026 workshop deck teaches patient cultivation without mentioning it.
Part IX, including section 329-130 as Act 46 rewrote it, has no end date that I found. Anyone planning a grow past 2027 should ask OMCCR how it reads the new section.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Whether the legislature changed any of these sections in the 2026 session. The statute compilation I read is dated January 5, 2026, the Registry's Laws and Rules page says new legislative action may not show until about November of the same year, and I did not search the 2026 session laws.
Whether OMCCR has published a rule or guidance for the new penalty section, or for the 2028 cultivator license, in anything I opened.
Whether the five-grow-site wording in OMCCR's caregiver sheet and the five-patient wording in the statute describe the same cap.
Whether the portal launched on September 30 as announced, and whether it changed registration numbers. No public page I read says either.
The rules text itself. The version OMCCR posts is the February 15, 2019 compilation of chapter 11-160. If the department amended the chapter later, I did not see it.
How a court would read any of this. I did not search case law for this piece, and the statutes themselves carry one note: a 2013 decision applying the rule of lenity to the transport provisions.
Your situation. A lease, an association rule or a neighbor can change what you may do. A separate piece covers renters and associations.

r: For a question about your own plants, ask OMCCR or a Hawaii attorney. Educational information, not legal advice. Education, not medical advice.

posts.title: Your Testimony Is Data
posts.subtitle: A Hawaii law and an agency rule come through two different doors. Here is how each one opens to the public, and how to testify before the 2027 legislative session begins on January 20.
posts.description: How a Hawaii law differs from an agency rule, and how to testify before the 2027 session opens on January 20, 2027. Education, not legal advice.

r: On January 1, 2025, caregivers in Hawaii's medical cannabis program, with some exceptions, lost the right to grow for their patients. The date was already in the statute as a sunset. On May 14, 2025, the governor signed Act 46, and Act 46 restored the right, retroactive to January 1, 2025.

I use that sequence because it shows the first thing to know about changing a rule in Hawaii: you have to know which door the change goes through. This article is education, not legal advice. It uses official pages only, all opened on October 11, 2026: the Constitution, the Hawaii Revised Statutes, the Session Laws, committee reports, the Legislature's testimony instructions, the Legislative Reference Bureau's Public Access Room, and two newsletters from the Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation (OMCCR). It reports no conversation with any official or any legislator.

blocks.x: Two doors: a law and a rule

r: A law starts as a bill. Only a legislator can introduce one, and bills can only be introduced early in a session, usually in the first week.
To become law, a bill must pass three readings in each chamber, on separate days, and the final version must be printed and available to members for at least 48 hours before the last vote.

Then the governor signs it, vetoes it or lets it become law. Enacted bills get an act number and are printed in the Session Laws of Hawaii, and permanent ones are folded into the Hawaii Revised Statutes (HRS).
The Public Access Room (PAR), a service of the Legislative Reference Bureau, says that on average only about 10 percent of the few thousand bills introduced each session make it through.
Most of the losses come from a missed deadline. A bill that never gets a hearing from the chair of its committee dies there.

A rule is a different thing, made in a different place. The Hawaii Administrative Procedure Act, HRS chapter 91, defines a rule as an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect that implements, interprets or prescribes law or policy. The chapter's definition of "agency" leaves out the legislative and judicial branches.

Rules are collected in the Hawaii Administrative Rules (HAR). PAR describes them as the operating procedures executive agencies set through rulemaking, to fill in the details of how a law will be carried out.
The rulemaking steps in HRS section 91-3 are short enough to list.

items: The agency gives at least 30 days' notice of a public hearing. The notice must say what the topic is, where the proposed text can be read and copied, and the date, time and place of the hearing.
The agency must afford all interested persons the opportunity to submit data, views or arguments, orally or in writing, and must fully consider all written and oral submissions.
After adoption, an interested person who asks can get a concise statement of the principal reasons for and against the agency's decision.

The governor must approve the rule. A rule takes effect ten days after it is filed with the lieutenant governor, unless a statute or the rule sets a later date, which cannot be more than 30 days after filing.
Any interested person can petition an agency to adopt, change or repeal a rule. Within 30 days the agency must either deny the petition in writing, with reasons, or start a rulemaking proceeding.

r: A current notice shows the form. The Department of Health's notice for a September 30, 2026 hearing on its lead-based paint rules, chapter 11-41, says what the rules cover, where the proposed text is posted and can be viewed in person, that copies are mailed on request for a per-page fee and postage, when and where the hearing is, that all interested parties may present information, comments and opinions, and that people who cannot attend may send written comments received by October 7.
It concerns another program. Chapter 91 asks the same elements of every state agency.
There are exceptions. An agency that finds imminent peril to public health, safety or morals can adopt an emergency rule on shorter notice, effective for no more than 120 days without renewal.
And a statute can exempt a set of rules from chapter 91 entirely. That is what happened with the dispensary program, which I come back to below.

The medical cannabis program shows the two doors working on a single number. Act 241 of 2025 says a certifying provider's fee may not exceed three times the fee the Department of Health charges for a registration certificate.
The multiplier of three is law. The registration fee it multiplies is a rule: HRS section 329-123 says the department may charge a fee "in an amount adopted by rules pursuant to chapter 91."
OMCCR's guidance sheet of September 18, 2025 puts the current registration fee at $35 for one year and $70 for two, which makes the cap $105 and $210.

If someone wants the cap to be different, they go to the Legislature. If someone wants the registration fee itself to be different, the door is a rulemaking hearing. Both are real routes, and they take different paperwork and different people.

Another example: OMCCR's November 2024 newsletter tells patients that every medical cannabis plant must carry an identification tag showing the registration number and expiration date, and it cites HAR section 11-160-31(b) as the source of the requirement.
That detail lives in a rule, so it is changed in a rule proceeding.

The Constitution fixes the first date. The Legislature "shall convene annually in regular session at 10:00 o'clock a.m. on the third Wednesday in January," and a regular session is limited to sixty days, not counting weekends, holidays and recess days.

In January 2027 the third Wednesday is January 20. That is a count from the Constitution's rule, not a date from a published calendar. When I opened PAR's Current Legislature page on October 11, 2026, it listed only the 2026 session calendar, and no 2027 calendar was up yet.
The pattern in the 2026 calendar was opening day on Wednesday, January 21, and a deadline to introduce bills on Wednesday, January 28, a week later.
OMCCR's December 2024 newsletter shows the same habit, naming Wednesday, January 15, 2025, as that session's opening day.
Odd-numbered years also start a new two-year term. PAR explains that after an election, everything starts afresh, with new legislators, new bills and a new biennium of two regular sessions.
PAR also notes that at the end of the second year, every bill that has not passed is dead. For a patient or caregiver, that means a bill you cared about in 2026 has to be introduced again in 2027.

The rule door has a date too, for one part of the program. The dispensary law, HRS chapter 329D, has been running on interim rules that are exempt from chapter 91. Act 46 moved the end of those interim rules from July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2027. The text says they stay in effect until that date or until rules are adopted under chapter 91, whichever happens first.
Chapter 91 means a public notice and a hearing. OMCCR's August 2025 newsletter says the office will engage with the community "through public listening sessions and the formal rulemaking process."
When I opened the Department of Health's page of proposed Title 11 rule changes on October 11, 2026, it listed hearings for other chapters and none for a cannabis chapter.
I found nothing that says when a hearing for the dispensary rules will be set.

blocks.x: How to testify at the Legislature

r: Testimony is a step you take on a bill that has a hearing. PAR is direct about it: you may offer testimony only when the measure has been scheduled for a hearing, and the instructions appear at the end of the hearing notice.
Before that point, the useful work is different. If you support a bill, you ask the committee chair to schedule it. If you oppose one, you can ask the chair not to.
The committee has to post a hearing notice at least 48 hours ahead. In the Senate, the first committee a bill is referred to posts at least 72 hours ahead.
Committees ask that testimony be submitted 24 hours before the hearing, and testimony that arrives after the deadline may still be accepted, at the chair's discretion.

The Legislature's own instructions for the 2026 session add two details: in the House, submitting 24 hours ahead is strongly encouraged, and in the Senate, a request to testify remotely must be in at least three hours before the hearing.

A House Judiciary and Hawaiian Affairs notice of hearing for February 21, 2025 prints the same rules at the bottom: submit testimony at least 24 hours before, testimony after that is stamped late and left to the chair's discretion, and the chair may set a per-testifier time limit.
Check the hearing notice for the current rules, because the instructions I read were written for 2025 and 2026.
The online route, step by step, from PAR's January 2026 handout and the Legislature's instructions:

items: Create a free account on the Legislature's website, capitol.hawaii.gov, and confirm it through the email the site sends you.
Log in and choose Submit Testimony. Enter the bill number with no spaces, periods or draft numbers. If no hearing is scheduled, the form will not let you continue.

Fill out the form. It shows the hearing date and time. You say whether you support, oppose or are offering comments, whether you speak as an individual or for an organization, and whether you will testify in person, by Zoom, or in writing only.
Upload a file (.doc, .docx, .pdf, .rtf, .txt or .odt, up to 20 MB) or type your testimony into the box. The site logs you out after 60 minutes, and a save button keeps your progress.
Review it, then submit. You cannot change testimony after you submit it.

r: If you cannot submit through the website because of a disability, the Legislature's instructions say to contact the committee directly.
PAR also helps by phone at (808) 587-0478 and in person at State Capitol Room 401.

What to say is up to you. PAR says there are no rules about what testimony should look or sound like. Its tips: put the bill number, the bill's title and your name first, say clearly whether you support or oppose, give factual accounts of the impact, tell a personal story, restate your request and keep it short. For oral testimony it suggests two to three minutes, a conversational tone, and not reading to the committee.
A one-page summary also helps when you talk to a legislator. PAR's template has six boxes: background, the issue, the solution, the ask, supporters and contact information.
OMCCR's December 2024 newsletter points patients to that template and to PAR's other handouts.
I mean the word in a plain sense. Testimony becomes a record that other people read, count and cite. I found three places it lands.

First, it is public. The Legislature's instructions say all testimony it receives is posted on its website and available to the public, and ask people not to include information they do not want disclosed.
PAR's handout repeats it: all testimony submitted is public and will appear online.
The 2025 hearing notice says the posting on the legislative website "should be considered when including personal information."
That is a reason to decide, before you write, how much of your health history belongs in a public file. A fact about how a rule works for you can carry the point without a diagnosis in it.

Second, committee reports say who was heard. The House Health Committee's report on the first House draft of the bill that became Act 241, dated February 3, 2025, says the committee received testimony in support from five organizations and comments from two state departments and a consulting firm.
The report names organizations and agencies. It does not show whether any individual patients testified, and I am not claiming they did or did not.

Third, the findings that open a law lean on numbers. Act 241 says the number of registered patients peaked at 35,444 in August 2021 and fell to 30,035 by November 2024, and it reads that drop as a sign that residents are shifting away from licensed dispensaries.

Act 46 cites a 2022 Department of Health survey in which 55 percent of patients said they got their cannabis only from a licensed dispensary, and concludes that up to 45 percent get it elsewhere, including by growing.

The conference committee report on Act 46 says some qualifying patients cannot cultivate on their own because of debilitating medical conditions, mobility impairments that make tending to plants difficult or impossible, or restrictions at their residence.
Those sentences are the kind a witness can supply: a specific effect, on a specific kind of person, with a number or a date attached.
For agency rules the data point is built into the statute. The agency "shall fully consider all written and oral submissions respecting the proposed rule."
A submission that cites the section it wants changed, says what happened under the current text and names the change it wants is easy for an agency to consider and to answer.

items: Make the account now. Registration is a one-time step and the confirmation email can land in a spam folder.
Check PAR's Current Legislature page for the 2027 calendar and handouts. In December 2024 it was the place OMCCR sent readers.

Write the one-pager. PAR says the drafting offices are busiest in December and early January, and that the best time to approach a legislator is the interim, starting with your own representative and senator.
Watch the two lists. For bills, the Legislature's site. For rules, the Lieutenant Governor's page of proposed changes to administrative rules, which links to each department's list.
When a hearing notice appears, read the instructions at the bottom of it first.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: The 2027 session calendar. As of October 11, 2026, PAR's page carried only 2026. January 20, 2027 is my count from the Constitution's rule.

Whether OMCCR has scheduled a chapter 91 hearing for the dispensary rules, or what happens if the interim rules reach July 1, 2027 with no final rules. The statute sets the end date. I found nothing on the plan.
Whether any bill on these topics will be introduced in 2027.
Whether individual patients testified on House Bill 302 or Senate Bill 1429. The one committee report I read names organizations and agencies, and I did not read the posted testimony.
Whether testimony changed any vote. Committee reports and findings show what the Legislature heard and cited. They do not show why a member voted a particular way.

The Legislature's own testimony page and Citizen's Guide on capitol.hawaii.gov. That site returned a security block (HTTP 403) to my requests, so I did not open those pages. I used the Legislature's data host, PAR and the Constitution instead.
Anything that has happened since October 11, 2026, including any 2026 session law not yet reflected on the HRS pages I opened.

r: This article is education, not legal advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney.

posts.description: What Acts 46, 241 and 269 of 2025 changed for Hawaii's 329 card: certification, telehealth, the fee cap, caregivers, a 2028 license and hemp seller registration.

r: The 329 card is the registration certificate the Department of Health issues to a qualifying patient. Its name comes from chapter 329 of the Hawaii Revised Statutes (HRS), part IX, and OMCCR, the Department's Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation, uses the same shorthand.

In 2025 the Legislature passed three laws that touch it. This article is education, not legal advice. I read the printed acts in the Session Laws of Hawaii, the current statute pages, the Legislature's committee reports and OMCCR's own guidance sheets, newsletters and program pages, all opened on October 11, 2026. Where OMCCR's summary and the statute word something differently, I say so and follow the statute.

Act 241 begins with a finding. Registered patients peaked in August 2021 at 35,444 and had fallen by more than fifteen percent to 30,035 by November 2024. The Legislature read that as a sign that residents were moving away from licensed dispensaries and getting cannabis elsewhere, "due to administrative barriers, delays in registering, and the ease and lower costs in obtaining cannabis elsewhere."

Act 46 begins with a different finding about patients who grow or have a caregiver grow, and I come to it below. Both findings are the Legislature's reading of the numbers. They are not measurements I checked.

blocks.x: Act 241: who can certify, and for what

r: Act 241 (House Bill 302) was approved on June 27, 2025, and took effect on July 1, 2025. One part of it, a new cultivator license, takes effect on January 1, 2028.

Before the Act, a qualifying patient was a person diagnosed with a debilitating medical condition. The statute's list of those conditions includes cancer, glaucoma, lupus, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, HIV, AIDS, and a chronic or debilitating condition that produces severe pain, severe nausea, seizures, severe and persistent muscle spasms, cachexia or post-traumatic stress disorder, along with any other condition the Department approves by rule.
Act 241 leaves that list alone. The conference committee report says the committee reverted to the existing definition of "debilitating medical condition."
What the Act adds is a second path and a third. The current definition of "qualifying patient" in HRS section 329-121 has three parts.

items: A person diagnosed with a debilitating medical condition by a physician or advanced practice registered nurse (APRN) who certifies in writing that the benefit is likely to outweigh the health risks.

A person diagnosed with a condition other than a debilitating medical condition by the person's "primary treating medical provider," who certifies in writing that the potential benefits are likely to outweigh the health risks.
A person receiving hospice care, when a licensed hospice provider certifies that.

r: The statute defines a primary treating medical provider as a physician or APRN located in Hawaii, with an active unrestricted Hawaii license, who within their scope of practice and competency is primarily responsible for the person's treatment and ongoing care, and who has determined that the potential benefits are likely to outweigh the risks.

OMCCR's guidance for providers adds that the provider must be either the primary care provider or a specialist who is the primary provider for the specific condition being certified, that a bona fide provider-patient relationship must exist, and that the written certification must document the diagnosis and show that risks and benefits were explained and understood.
OMCCR's August 2025 newsletter summarizes the change as "any condition being actively treated by a medical provider."

The statute does not use those words. It says a condition other than a debilitating one, diagnosed by the person's primary treating medical provider. For a patient, the difference is practical: the person who certifies has to be the one primarily responsible for your care for that condition.

Before Act 241, HRS section 453-1.3(c) said that for prescribing opiates or for certifying a patient for the medical use of cannabis, a physician-patient relationship could be established only after an in-person consultation. Act 241 deletes the cannabis words from that sentence.

It also adds, in sections 329-123(a) and 329-126(b), language that nothing in the medical cannabis part requires the provider-patient relationship to be established by an initial in-person consultation.
OMCCR's telehealth guidance, issued September 18, 2025, says patients may use telehealth for an initial certification or a renewal "beginning September 18th, 2025."
The Act's own effective date is July 1, 2025. I did not find an explanation of the gap in the texts I opened, so I report both dates. The guidance also keeps the standards in place:

items: The provider must be physically located in Hawaii at the time of the appointment.
Telehealth must meet the same standard of practice as an in-person visit, with a documented evaluation that includes history and a discussion of physical symptoms.
Relying only on an online questionnaire does not meet the standard of care.
The provider keeps complete medical records and must establish a bona fide provider-patient relationship.

r: I have a spinal condition that affects my arms and hands, so I read this part of Act 241 with limited hand function in mind. A required first visit in a clinic asks for a trip and a way through the door before any care starts. For a person with limited hand function, both can be hard. A visit by video starts at home. The Act removes the first-visit rule and keeps the evaluation, the records and the Hawaii-located provider.

Act 241 limits what a certifying provider can charge. The fee for a written certification "shall not exceed an amount equal to three times the amount of the fee charged by the department of health to issue a registration certificate."

The statute states no dollar amount. OMCCR's guidance, also issued September 18, 2025, puts the current Department fee at $35 for a one-year certification and $70 for two years, which makes the cap $105 for one year and $210 for two.

The same guidance lists what the capped fee must cover: the whole evaluation, including an explanation of risks and benefits; completion of the written certification on OMCCR's approved form; and maintenance of the medical records tied to it. Providers must tell a patient the certification fee and any additional fee before the evaluation. A provider may charge separately for other medical services unrelated to certification, if those are disclosed first.
The registration fee that the cap multiplies is set by rule, not by statute. HRS section 329-123(b) lets the Department charge a fee "in an amount adopted by rules pursuant to chapter 91."
The cap is the Legislature's number. The base is the Department's.

blocks.x: The Department can look at the records

r: Act 241 also gives the Department authority to inspect a qualifying patient's medical records held by the physician, APRN or hospice provider who issued the certification. It may suspend or revoke the ability to issue certifications of a provider who refuses inspection, or whose records do not meet the chapter's requirements.
OMCCR's newsletter says the office may start a review when patients raise serious concerns about their care.

For a patient, the practical point is that the medical record supporting a certification is something the Department can ask to see, which is one more reason to confirm that the provider keeps records as the guidance requires.
Act 46 (Senate Bill 1429) was approved on May 14, 2025. Its caregiver sections apply retroactively to January 1, 2025.
Before that, a sunset in HRS section 329-130 had ended caregiver cultivation after December 31, 2024, with exceptions for minors and for islands without a dispensary.

The Act removes the sunset. Under the current statute, a qualifying patient may get medical cannabis only from a licensed dispensary, by growing an amount within the "adequate supply" limit, or from a primary caregiver who grows that amount for the patient. Each location used to cultivate cannabis may be used for not more than five qualifying patients.
The caregiver rules changed in three ways.

items: A primary caregiver was limited to one patient, with an exception for parents of several minors. The statute now says a caregiver is responsible for not more than five qualifying patients at a time.
The Department may register up to two primary caregivers for a minor patient, if both are the minor's parent, guardian or legal custodian.

The Department can now penalize violations of this part of the law. The fine is up to $5,000 per violation, and each day a violation continues is a separate offense. The Department may issue an administrative penalty with a cease and desist order or an order for corrective action. These become final 20 calendar days after notice unless the person asks in writing for a contested case hearing under chapter 91.

r: The Legislature gave reasons. Act 46's findings say some patients may not be able to grow because of limitations such as disability or lack of space, and cite a 2022 Department of Health survey in which 55 percent of patients said they got cannabis only from a licensed dispensary. The Act reads that as meaning up to 45 percent get it from other sources, including cultivation.

The conference committee report adds that some patients cannot cultivate on their own because of debilitating conditions, mobility impairments that make tending to plants difficult or impossible, or restrictions at their residence.

One wording difference is worth knowing. The statute limits each growing location by number of qualifying patients, not more than five. OMCCR's caregiver guidance sheet says "no single location shall be permitted to have more than five grow sites registered to it."

Those are different limits, and the sheet says it is informational and does not replace legal or other regulatory advice. I follow the statute here and flag the sheet's wording as something to ask OMCCR about.

blocks.x: Act 241, Part IV: a cultivator license in 2028

r: Part IV of Act 241 adds a new section to chapter 329D, the dispensary law. Beginning January 1, 2028, "it shall be unlawful for any person to cultivate cannabis without a license issued by the department pursuant to this section." A licensee may acquire and cultivate cannabis plants, seeds, cuttings or clones, and distribute plants and flower to a medical cannabis dispensary. The Department issues no more than one license per person, and a licensee must meet the production facility and processing requirements of chapter 329D.
The conference committee removed an earlier cap on the number of licenses and an earlier limit on plant canopy size.

OMCCR's August 2025 newsletter describes the license as a way to increase the variety of flower and products at dispensaries, to be rolled out in 2028, with outreach and program development over the following year.

Here is a question the text leaves open. The new section begins "notwithstanding section 329D-24." Section 329D-24 says nothing in chapter 329D shall be construed to prohibit a qualifying patient or primary caregiver from cultivating or possessing an adequate supply under part IX of chapter 329.

The Act says "any person." The texts I opened do not say whether registered patients and caregivers are inside or outside the 2028 license requirement. I found no OMCCR statement either way. That is a question for the Department or for a Hawaii attorney, and one to watch in the rulemaking OMCCR says is coming.

Dispensaries' retail locations may now sell hemp products and accessories to the medical use of cannabis, including rolling papers, rolling trays, grinders and vaporizers, though not in the waiting room.

Part II makes unlicensed operation of a dispensary a class C felony, and a misdemeanor for operators of search platforms, web hosting services and social media platforms that post advertising for unlicensed cannabis sales, with an affirmative defense for those that requested, examined and reasonably relied on a license that appeared to be issued by the Department.
Part III appropriates $750,000 for fiscal year 2025 to 2026, and the same sum for 2026 to 2027, to the Attorney General for nuisance enforcement and six positions.
OMCCR's newsletter calls this a "new nuisance abatement unit"; the text amends the purpose of an existing drug nuisance abatement unit and funds positions.

Act 269 (House Bill 1482) was approved on July 2, 2025, and took effect on July 1, 2025. It adds a registry of manufactured hemp product distributors and retailers to chapter 328G. Beginning January 1, 2026, no distributor or retailer may sell or offer manufactured hemp products without a certificate of registration. The application fee is $50, the certificate is valid for five years, and renewal costs $50. Hemp processors with a valid permit are issued a certificate without those fees. The Department must post a current list of registrants.
The Act defines "sale" to include orders placed by phone, mail, catalog, digital application or the internet, and online registrants must display a digital copy of the certificate on the website.

OMCCR's hemp page says the requirement covers online sellers outside Hawaii, that the application opened January 1, 2026, that OMCCR allowed a grace period, and that enforcement began on July 1, 2026.
OMCCR's September/October 2025 newsletter says "all businesses that sell hemp products in Hawai'i must register."
The statute carves out two product types: the registration section does not apply to sales of topically applied products or tinctures. Tinctures may not be sold to people under 21.
OMCCR's retailer and distributor FAQ lists the same exceptions.
Unregistered selling is a misdemeanor if done recklessly, and a class C felony when it follows a conviction within five years. Penalties under chapter 328G run up to $10,000 per offense.

items: Dates: Act 46, May 14, 2025 (caregiver sections retroactive to January 1, 2025). Act 269, July 2, 2025, effective July 1, 2025. Act 241, June 27, 2025, effective July 1, 2025, with Part IV effective January 1, 2028.

Statute first. OMCCR's sheets and newsletters are summaries. The Registry Program Updates page lists the telehealth and fee cap guidance under September 18, 2025, and the primary treating provider and caregiver guidance under December 1, 2025.
Rules come next. The Department may still adopt rules under these acts, and rules go through a different door than statutes. If you want to be heard on one, watch for a notice of public hearing.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Why OMCCR's telehealth and fee cap guidance start on September 18, 2025, when the Act took effect July 1, 2025.
How the 2028 cultivator license applies, if at all, to registered patients and caregivers growing under part IX of chapter 329.
Whether the caregiver guidance sheet's "five grow sites" wording or the statute's five qualifying patients controls in practice.

What OMCCR's rules will say. The Department's list of proposed Title 11 rule changes showed no cannabis chapter, and I did not read the January 28, 2026 copy of the hemp interim rules, chapter 11-37, that OMCCR's hemp page links.
Any change from the 2026 legislative session. The statute pages I opened show amendments through Acts 46 and 241 of 2025, and the online Revised Statutes can lag behind new session laws.
How many patients, caregivers or providers have used any of these changes. I found no OMCCR figures.

r: This article is education, not legal advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney.

posts.title: December, Seeds and the Home Grower
posts.subtitle: What the new federal hemp definition says about seeds, what Hawaii already says, and the questions neither text answers
posts.seoTitle: December, Seeds and the Home Grower
posts.description: The federal hemp definition changes on November 12 and December 11, 2026. What the texts say about hemp seeds, shipping and Hawaii law, and what they leave open.

r: A sentence about seeds in a federal funding law is scheduled to start working on December 11, 2026.

It sits in section 781 of Public Law 119-37, the agriculture funding law signed on November 12, 2025. The sentence says that "hemp" does not include any viable seeds from a cannabis plant that is over 0.3 percent total THC in the plant, counting THCA, on a dry weight basis.
Until December 11, the 2018 Farm Bill wording still defines hemp: 0.3 percent delta-9 THC, dry weight. Unless Congress acts again, that is the calendar.

This article is education, not legal advice. Questions about seeds, shipping and home growing belong with a licensed attorney who knows the law of the state where you live. What follows is a reading of the texts I opened, a list of the ones I could not open, and the questions the texts leave unanswered.

blocks.x: Two dates, and neither has arrived

r: The law that rewrites the definition says it starts "365 days after the enactment," which is November 12, 2026.

A second law, Public Law 119-103, signed on September 2, 2026, changes that for most of the new definition. Its section 2019 says that until December 11, 2026, the amendments from section 781 "shall only apply" to two kinds of product, both described by one phrase: cannabinoids that "are not capable of being naturally produced" by the plant.

Put the two laws together and you get two steps. On November 12, 2026, the exclusion for products with those non-natural cannabinoids starts. On December 11, 2026, the rest of the new definition starts, including the switch from delta-9 THC to total THC with THCA counted, and the seed exclusion. The Congressional Research Service describes the same split in its September 28, 2026 update.
The same continuing resolution funds the government only until December 11, 2026, unless an earlier event ends the funding first.

That is a coincidence of dates I would not lean on. CRS lists bills that would delay the new definition for two more years, bills that would repeal the change, and bills that would rewrite it. It also says the House-passed agriculture funding bill for fiscal year 2027 carries no delay.
I cannot tell you which way that goes. I can tell you the dates in this article come from texts as they stood on October 11, 2026, and anyone relying on them should check Congress.gov first.

blocks.x: What the 2018 law said about seeds

r: The 2018 Farm Bill defined hemp as the cannabis plant "and any part of that plant, including the seeds thereof," with a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis.
In the same law, Congress changed the Controlled Substances Act so that "marihuana" does not include hemp.
The Controlled Substances Act still defines marijuana to include "the seeds thereof," and its other exclusions include "the sterilized seed of such plant which is incapable of germination."

In 2020 the Drug Enforcement Administration explained what the change meant for seeds. Viable hemp seed had been a Schedule I controlled substance before the Farm Bill, it said, and after the Farm Bill it was no longer subject to those Schedule I requirements "as long as the material contains less than the 0.3% limit."

Read the 2018 sentence slowly and a gap shows. It applies the 0.3 percent test to hemp, and hemp includes seeds, but it does not say whose concentration counts when the thing in your hand is a seed: the seed's own, or the plant's it came from. I did not find that answer in any of the texts I opened.

The 2025 text keeps "the seeds thereof" in the main definition. Then it adds exclusions, and the first is about seeds. Hemp "does not include any viable seeds from a Cannabis sativa L. plant that exceeds a total tetrahydrocannabinols concentration (including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid) of 0.3 percent in the plant on a dry weight basis."

Two things stand out. First, the test now looks at the plant, with the words "in the plant." That answers the gap in the 2018 sentence by naming the parent. Second, the exclusion names only viable seeds. The Controlled Substances Act has long treated sterilized seed that cannot germinate differently from other seed.
The new law does not define "viable."

The same section treats seed as hemp in other places. It defines industrial hemp to include hemp grown for the use of the whole grain, oil, cake, nut or hull of the seeds, hemp grown for microgreens from seeds that do not exceed the threshold, and hemp grown for a viable seed "produced solely for the production or manufacture" of those materials.
So the same statute treats two kinds of viable seed differently. One kind is hemp. The other is not.

What happens to a seed that falls outside the definition? CRS says that from the effective date, products excluded by these provisions "are not to be deemed hemp products and would instead be subject to regulation under the CSA as marijuana."
A CRS legal sidebar calls the change "an exception to the exceptions."
The Controlled Substances Act text points the same way: its marijuana definition includes seeds and carves out hemp, so a seed that is no longer hemp is back inside the first part of the definition.

What the new text does not do is explain how a seller or buyer would know a seed's parent plant tested over or under 0.3 percent. I found no testing rule, labeling rule or record-keeping rule for that in section 781. Congress also told the Food and Drug Administration to publish lists of cannabinoids within 90 days of enactment, and CRS reported on September 28, 2026 that the lists had not been published.
Those lists bear on the cannabinoid exclusions. They do not speak to seeds.

CRS also says it remains unclear if and how federal law enforcement will enforce the new definition, and it notes that the Department of Justice has generally not prioritized small-scale violations or activity that complies with state law.
I will not guess at enforcement. The record I opened does not show it.

blocks.x: Moving seeds across state lines and borders

r: Several federal provisions come up whenever someone asks about shipping hemp seed. Each has limits.

Section 10114 of the 2018 Farm Bill says nothing in that title "prohibits the interstate commerce of hemp." It also says no State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products "produced in accordance with" the hemp subtitle "through" the State.
The word "through" matters, and so does the phrase about how the hemp was produced.

Section 737 of the 2026 agriculture funding law is a limit on money. None of the funds in that act or any other act may be used to prohibit the transportation, processing, sale or use of hemp, or "seeds of such plant," grown in accordance with the farm bill hemp programs, within or outside the State where it is grown.

A funding limit lasts as long as the funding does. The continuing resolution keeps funding the programs of the 2026 agriculture act "under the authority and conditions provided in such Acts," until December 11, 2026 at the latest.
Whether the limit still protects anything after that, and whether it reaches a seed that has been excluded from hemp, are questions for a licensed attorney. The texts do not answer them.

The Federal Seed Act is a different kind of law. The Agricultural Marketing Service calls it a truth-in-labeling law for agricultural and vegetable seed shipped in interstate commerce, with required label information such as purity, germination, and the name and address of the shipper.
Its hemp FAQ says all seed sold in the United States requires a label.
In its 2021 hemp rule, USDA chose not to run a hemp seed certification program and recommended varietal certification under the Federal Seed Act instead.

For imports, the same rule says the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service regulates the importation of all seeds for planting, and hemp seeds from Canada need either a phytosanitary certificate or a Federal Seed Analysis Certificate.
DEA's 2020 rule ended its own import permit requirement for viable hemp seed under the limit.
None of those texts says what happens to the rules for a seed that, after December 11, is no longer hemp.

I did not read the shipping rules of the Postal Service or private carriers, the Customs and Border Protection guidance, or Hawaii's plant import rules. Anyone moving seeds should have those read by someone qualified.

blocks.x: What Hawaii already says about seeds

r: Hawaii has not waited for Washington. The Department of Health's hemp rules, Chapter 11-37 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules, say that no person shall sell, hold for sale, offer or distribute hemp leaf, hemp floral material or "viable hemp seeds," except to a hemp producer holding a USDA license or to a permitted hemp processor.
The department's own FAQ, current as of June 23, 2026, lists "all viable hemp seeds" among the products prohibited for sale in Hawaii, "regardless of the labeled percentage" of THC or THCA.
The statute that defines the state's hemp products also leaves seeds out. A "manufactured hemp product" under the hemp processor chapter does not include living hemp plants or viable seeds.
Growing hemp commercially requires a USDA license, and a person who grows hemp without one faces a civil fine of up to $10,000 for each separate offense.

State criminal law adds another layer. Hawaii's penal code defines "marijuana" to include "the seeds." Its hemp exceptions turn on who holds the hemp, meaning a USDA license holder or a person authorized under state law to process hemp, or on a finished product that has no viable seeds and tests at or under 0.3 percent delta-9 THC after heat conversion.
They do not name a loose viable seed in other hands. What that means for a particular person is a question for an attorney.

Act 269 of 2025, the hemp seller registration law, does not mention seeds. It requires registration of certain distributors and retailers of manufactured hemp products, and seeds are outside that term.

There is also a clock. The Hawaii Revised Statutes notes on the legislature's website say the hemp processor chapter and the commercial hemp production part are repealed on July 1, 2027. The same notes mark the state's hemp definition as repealed on that date and its marijuana definition for repeal and reenactment.
I do not know what the legislature will do. The federal seed sentence and the state's seed rules both sit on calendars that change in the next nine months.

Hawaii's medical cannabis law defines "medical use" to include the "acquisition, possession, cultivation, use, distribution, or transportation" of cannabis for a qualifying patient. It says "cannabis" has the same meaning as "marijuana" in the sections of the code I cited above.

The Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation says qualifying patients may obtain medical cannabis only in three ways: from a licensed dispensary, by growing personally within the limits set for an adequate supply, or from a registered primary caregiver who grows for them.
That guidance does not mention seeds. OMCCR's public Know Before You Grow deck from March 7, 2026 has a section on choosing seeds and notes that cloning can reduce the need to buy new ones.
The pages I read do not say where seeds may be lawfully obtained.
State protection also has a ceiling. OMCCR's own public FAQ says that all cannabis is illegal under federal law.

I want to be plain about what I am not saying. I am not saying a patient may or may not buy, receive or ship a seed. I am saying the texts I opened name three lawful sources of medical cannabis, name a state prohibition on selling viable hemp seed, and leave the patient's seed question without an answer.
If you grow, plan to grow, or advise people who do, these are the questions the texts leave open.

items: Which test applies on the day a seed is sold or received: the 2018 delta-9 test, or the new total THC test on the parent plant?
Who has to be able to show a seed's parent plant tested at or under 0.3 percent, and how?
Do section 10114 and section 737 protect a seed shipment, and do they reach a seed that has been excluded from hemp?
How does Hawaii's rule against selling viable hemp seed fit with a registered patient's right to acquire cannabis?
What do carriers, the Postal Service and Customs treat as a lawful seed shipment, before and after December 11?
What happens on July 1, 2027, if Hawaii's hemp chapter and definitions are repealed and not replaced?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Whether Congress changes the December 11, 2026 date before it arrives.
Whose THC concentration counts for a seed under the 2018 sentence.
How "viable" is defined, and how a parent plant's test result would reach a seed buyer.
How federal agencies will enforce the seed exclusion.
Whether section 10114 and section 737 reach seeds excluded from hemp.
The shipping rules of carriers, the Postal Service and Customs, and Hawaii's plant import rules. I did not read them.
Where a Hawaii patient may lawfully get seeds. The state texts I opened do not say.
What Hawaii's legislature does about the July 1, 2027 repeal dates.
The current text of USDA's hemp rule in the Code of Federal Regulations. I read the January 19, 2021 final rule and the current AMS FAQ, and I could not open the current regulation text.

posts.title: Renters, HOAs and the Patient Gardener
posts.subtitle: What Hawaii's lease, condominium and planned community statutes say about medical cannabis, what they leave out, and where a patient who rents has to look next.
posts.seoTitle: Renters, HOAs and the Patient Gardener
posts.description: Hawaii's rental, condominium and planned community statutes on medical cannabis, read in full, with what they say and what they leave open about growing at home.

r: Educational information, not legal advice. Education, not medical advice. This piece reads public texts. It cannot tell you what your lease, your association's documents or a court would do in your case.

A registered patient who rents, or who owns a unit in a condominium or a planned community, asks a plain question: can I grow here? Hawaii's medical cannabis chapter, chapter 329, says who may grow and where the grow site goes. It does not answer the landlord or association part. That part lives in three other places in the Hawaii Revised Statutes: the landlord-tenant code in chapter 521, the condominium law in chapter 514B and the planned community law in chapter 421J. This piece reads those sections in full, says what each one covers, and says plainly where the text goes silent.

I read the statute sections on October 11, 2026. The legislature's main website refused my automated request that day, so I read each section on its data site, data.capitol.hawaii.gov. The statute listing there carries a compilation date of January 5, 2026, which includes the 2025 acts. I did not check the 2026 session laws. The one federal source is a 2011 housing memo that the Registry posts on its own site.

Part IX of chapter 329 governs medical use of cannabis. Section 329-121 defines "medical use" as the acquisition, possession, cultivation, use, distribution or transportation of cannabis or related paraphernalia to ease the symptoms of a patient's condition. Cultivation sits inside that definition, and the definition is written for "this part."

The Registry's Growing Cannabis page says a patient's grow site must be one of three places: the patient's residence, the designated caregiver's residence, or another site that the patient or caregiver owns or controls. The site must be listed on the 329 card.
The department's rule says the same and has the patient swear that the patient or caregiver resides at, owns or controls the grow site.

Nothing in sections 329-121 through 329-130 that I read says what a landlord or an association may forbid. Part IX contains a single pointer. A cross-reference at the head of the part reads "Medical cannabis; tenant use; eviction, see §521-39."
That is where the rental rule lives.
Section 521-39, "Medical cannabis; tenant use; eviction," is one long sentence plus a proviso. Here it is in plain order.

A provision in a rental agreement that allows eviction of a tenant who has a valid certificate for the medical use of cannabis, as provided in section 329-123, "in any form," is void. There is one exception. The provision is not void if the rental agreement allows eviction for smoking tobacco and the medical cannabis is used by smoking. The section then adds that it "shall not apply" where the articles of incorporation, declaration, bylaws, administrative rules, house rules, association documents or a similar document of a condominium property regime or planned community association prohibits the medical use of cannabis.
Four things follow from the words themselves.
First, the rule protects a tenant who holds a valid certificate. The statute ties that term to section 329-123, the registration section. A tenant without a valid certificate does not fall under it.

Second, the smoking carve-out has two conditions, and both have to be true. The lease has to let the landlord evict for tobacco smoking, and the cannabis has to be smoked. A smoking ban in a lease reaches cannabis smoke only when the lease already lets the landlord evict for tobacco smoking. If the cannabis is not smoked, the exception does not apply on its face.
Third, the statute says a clause is void. It does not describe a remedy, a hearing or a penalty.

Fourth, the last sentence is a large exception. In a condominium or planned community whose own documents prohibit the medical use of cannabis, section 521-39 does not apply. A tenant in such a building cannot lean on this section.

The two association statutes use matching language. Section 514B-113 covers condominiums and section 421J-16 covers planned community associations. Each is titled "Medical cannabis; discrimination." Each says that a provision in the association's governing documents allowing any of the discriminatory practices listed in section 515-3(a)(1) to (7) against a person residing in a unit who has a valid certificate for the medical use of cannabis is void, unless the documents prohibit the smoking of tobacco and the medical cannabis is used by smoking. Each adds that nothing in the section diminishes the association's duty to provide reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities under section 515-3(a)(9). Each points to the other as a similar provision. Both were last amended in 2023, according to their history notes.

Section 515-3 is the fair housing statute. The practices in paragraphs (1) to (7) include refusing to engage in a real estate transaction with a person, discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a transaction or in the services and facilities that come with it, refusing to receive or transmit a bona fide offer, refusing to negotiate, misrepresenting that property is unavailable, listing property with the understanding that a person may be discriminated against, and requiring a test for human immunodeficiency virus. Paragraph (9) requires reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a housing accommodation.

The sections do not say what happens when a medical patient's rights under 514B-113 or 421J-16 collide with an association rule that bans a particular use, such as growing plants in a unit. I found no text that answers it.

blocks.x: What none of these sections says

r: None of the three housing sections mentions growing. They speak of a tenant or resident "who has a valid certificate for the medical use of cannabis." Chapter 329 defines "medical use" to include cultivation, so a reader can argue that the housing sections borrow that meaning. But the chapter 329 definition says it applies "as used in this part," meaning part IX.
The housing sections do not say they adopt it. I found nothing in the statutes that settles the point, and I did not search court decisions, so I cannot say whether a Hawaii court has.

The sections also do not address the tension between 521-39's proviso and the association statutes. Section 521-39 says it does not apply where association documents prohibit the medical use of cannabis. Sections 514B-113 and 421J-16 void certain discriminatory provisions in association documents. A reader can hold both texts in view. The statutes themselves do not say which controls when an association's documents prohibit medical use outright, and I do not guess.
In 2017, Act 170 changed all three sections, along with others, but only to replace the word "marijuana" with "cannabis." It did not add or remove a right.

blocks.x: The ordinary lease rules still apply

r: Landlord-tenant law has its own test for restrictions on how a tenant uses a home. Section 521-52 says a tenant must comply with obligations or restrictions on the use, occupancy and maintenance of the dwelling unit and premises if they were brought to the tenant's attention when the tenant entered the rental agreement, or later with the tenant's written consent if they substantially change the bargain. No such restriction is enforceable unless it promotes the convenience, safety or welfare of tenants or protects the landlord's property from abusive use, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies to all tenants in a fair manner, and is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do or not do. For a condominium unit, the tenant must also comply with the association's bylaws.

Section 521-51(8) adds that a tenant must comply with obligations and restrictions that meet the 521-52 test and that the landlord can show are reasonably necessary to preserve the property and protect people.

Section 521-72 describes what a landlord does when a tenant breaks a rule: written notice, at least ten days to fix it, and then a summary proceeding for possession if the breach continues. The ten-day cure period does not apply when the breach causes or threatens damage to a person or violates certain tenant duties in 521-51.

Whether a lease clause that bans growing plants meets the 521-52 test for a registered patient, or collides with 521-39, is not answered by any text I read. The text gives the factors a court would weigh. It does not apply them.

Hawaii's criminal code has a provision that matters to anyone who grows at a place they do not own. Section 712-1249.5 defines commercial promotion of marijuana in the second degree. One way to commit it is to cultivate any marijuana plant on land owned by another person, including land owned by the government or another entity, unless the person has the owner's express permission, an ownership interest in the land, or a legal right to occupy the land. The offense is a class B felony.
A higher degree, in section 712-1249.4, covers larger numbers of plants on another person's land.
OMCCR's Laws and Rules page lists both sections as the consequences of cultivation that falls outside the program.

For a tenant, the phrase to read is "a legal right to occupy the land." A lease gives a legal right to occupy the dwelling and its grounds as the lease defines them. The statute does not say whether a lease that forbids cultivation affects that right, and it does not say what counts as the land when a tenant plants in a shared yard or a common area. I did not find a court decision on the point. Section 329-125 also lets a patient raise medical use as an affirmative defense, but only with strict compliance with part IX.
Part IX gives two other routes. A patient does not have to grow at the patient's own home. The grow site may be the caregiver's residence or another site the patient or caregiver owns or controls.

Since Act 46 of 2025, a primary caregiver may cultivate an adequate supply for each patient the caregiver serves, up to five patients, and each location used to cultivate cannabis may be used for not more than five qualifying patients.
A patient may also skip cultivation and buy from a licensed dispensary, which section 329-130 lists as the first lawful source.
None of that removes the housing question. A caregiver's grow site is also somebody's home or land, and the same questions apply there.

blocks.x: A federal layer for public housing

r: The Registry's Laws and Rules page links a 2011 memo from the Department of Housing and Urban Development to public housing agencies. It says federal law prohibits new admissions of medical marijuana users to public housing and to the Housing Choice Voucher program, because the Controlled Substances Act lists marijuana as a Schedule I drug and the Quality Housing and Work Responsibility Act of 1998 requires standards against admission based on illegal drug use. For current residents, the memo says housing agencies have discretion and must adopt a written policy.

I did not check whether HUD has replaced the memo since 2011, and the memo does not speak to any other kind of housing. A patient in subsidized housing should ask the housing agency for its written policy.
The Registry's Laws and Rules page also says Hawaii's smoke-free law, chapter 328J, applies directly to smoking or vaping cannabis.
I did not open the housing-related parts of that chapter. The lease statute's tobacco clause is the only smoking rule I read in full.
These are questions the texts raise, not legal conclusions.

items: Does my lease or my association's documents say anything about growing plants or about medical cannabis? Where exactly?
Was that language shown to me when I signed, or in writing since? Section 521-52 turns on that.
Do the association's documents prohibit the medical use of cannabis? Section 521-39 says it stops applying if they do.
Does my lease let the landlord evict for smoking tobacco? If not, the smoking carve-out in 521-39 does not apply as written.
Who owns the land my plants would sit on, and do I have a legal right to occupy that part of it?
Is the grow site on my 329 card an address I live at, own or control?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Any court decision applying sections 521-39, 514B-113 or 421J-16, or the criminal provision on land owned by another, to a medical patient who grows. I did not search case law.
Whether the 2026 legislature changed any of these sections. The compilation I read is dated January 5, 2026, and I did not search the 2026 session laws.
How the proviso in 521-39 interacts with 514B-113 and 421J-16 when association documents prohibit medical use.
Whether "medical use" in the housing sections includes cultivation.
What any particular lease or association document says. Governing documents differ, and this piece cannot read yours.
Whether HUD's 2011 memo is still its current position.
The text of the Department of Health's guidance, if any, on tenants. I found none on its public pages.

r: Educational information, not legal advice. Education, not medical advice. A Hawaii attorney or a tenant legal aid office can read your documents. This piece cannot.
