posts.title: Where Hemp Ends
posts.subtitle: How federal and Hawaii law draw the hemp line, where both lines are about to move, and what the texts leave open
posts.description: The federal hemp line moves on November 12 and December 11, 2026. How the 2018 and 2025 definitions differ, what Hawaii allows and bans, and what the texts leave open.

r: Hawaii's health department tells consumers that hemp and cannabis are one plant, separated by a legal line.

That line is about to move twice. The first move is scheduled for November 12, 2026, and the second for December 11, 2026, under two federal laws. Until then, the 2018 Farm Bill wording governs most of the definition: 0.3 percent delta-9 THC on a dry weight basis. Unless Congress acts again, those are the dates.

This article is education, not legal advice. It reads the federal definition and Hawaii's hemp law side by side, says which texts I opened, and lists what they leave open. Anyone who sells, buys or makes hemp products should have a licensed attorney read the current text for their situation.

The 2018 Farm Bill defined hemp as the cannabis plant and any part of it, "including the seeds thereof and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers," with a delta-9 THC concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis.
The same law changed the Controlled Substances Act so that "marihuana" does not include hemp.

Delta-9 THC was the only compound in the test. The Drug Enforcement Administration read the law this way in 2020: a cannabis derivative, extract or product that exceeds the 0.3 percent delta-9 limit is a Schedule I controlled substance, even if the plant it came from was at or under 0.3 percent.

The Congressional Research Service adds that the delta-9 test left room for argument about other cannabinoids. It reports that DEA took the position that compounds not found in the plant, such as THCO, did not qualify for the hemp exception, and that two federal appeals courts held that THCO and delta-8 THC fell within the 2018 definition.

The farm side of the program already looked past delta-9. The Agricultural Marketing Service's FAQ says USDA hemp testing must consider the potential conversion of THCA into THC, and that the result reports the total available THC from the sum of THC and THCA.
So THCA was never invisible to growers who hold a USDA license. What changed in 2025 is the statutory test for the products that reach consumers.

Section 781 of Public Law 119-37, signed November 12, 2025, replaces the definition. Hemp is still the plant and its parts, including the seeds, but the concentration test is now "a total tetrahydrocannabinols concentration (including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid) of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis."
The new text then does three things.

First, it says hemp includes industrial hemp, and it defines industrial hemp by use: stalk and fiber, whole grain, oil, cake, nut and hull from the seed, microgreens, research plants that never enter commerce, and viable seed made only for those uses.

Second, it writes a list of exclusions. Hemp does not include viable seeds from a plant over the 0.3 percent total THC threshold. It does not include intermediate hemp-derived cannabinoid products that contain cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally make, or cannabinoids the plant can make that were synthesized or manufactured outside the plant, or more than 0.3 percent combined total THC and similar cannabinoids. It does not include intermediate products marketed or sold as a final product or directly to a consumer for personal or household use. And it does not include final hemp-derived cannabinoid products that contain non-natural or outside-the-plant cannabinoids, or that exceed a fixed cap on combined THC and similar cannabinoids per retail container. The statute states that cap as a number, in new paragraph (1)(C)(iv)(III) of section 297A as amended by section 781. I describe it in words and leave the number to the text.

Third, it hands part of the work to the executive branch. "Similar effects" is to be determined by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and the law told the Food and Drug Administration to publish lists of naturally produced cannabinoids and further detail on the word "container" within 90 days of enactment.
CRS reported on September 28, 2026 that the lists had not been published.
CRS says that from the effective date, products excluded by these provisions "are not to be deemed hemp products and would instead be subject to regulation under the CSA as marijuana."
It describes the amendment as "an exception to the exceptions."
It also says it remains unclear if and how federal law enforcement will enforce the new definition.

blocks.x: Two dates, and what each one starts

r: Section 781 takes effect "365 days after the enactment," which is November 12, 2026.

Public Law 119-103, signed September 2, 2026, adds section 2019. It says that until December 11, 2026, the section 781 amendments "shall only apply" to products described in two paragraphs, both about cannabinoids "not capable of being naturally produced" by the plant.

So the schedule has two steps. On November 12, 2026, the exclusion for products with non-natural cannabinoids starts. On December 11, 2026, the rest of the new definition starts: the total THC test, the seed exclusion, the other product exclusions and the per-container cap.
Until the second date, the 2018 wording still decides what hemp is for everything else.

I would not treat either date as certain. CRS lists bills that would delay the new definition for two more years, bills that would repeal it, and bills that would rewrite it with a higher threshold, a state-defined line or a new product framework. It also says the House-passed fiscal year 2027 agriculture funding bill contains no delay.
The continuing resolution that moved the date also funds the government only until December 11, 2026.
Check Congress.gov before relying on a date from this article.

Hawaii draws its own line, and it is narrower than the federal one. The Department of Health's consumer FAQ says only "manufactured hemp products" may be sold, and lists the allowed forms for humans or animals: products applied to skin or hair, and edible gummies, tablets, capsules, powders, softgels, gelcaps, oil-based tinctures and beverages.
Each must meet total THC limits per serving and per container, a ceiling of 0.3 percent total THC by weight, laboratory testing, child-resistant packaging and labeling rules.
I leave the figures to the rule text. They are stated in milligrams and apply to sellers.

Hawaii also defines the test in its own words. The state's hemp definition uses delta-9 THC at not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis, "as measured post-decarboxylation or by other similarly reliable methods."
For manufactured hemp products, the rule defines total THC as the sum of THCA, adjusted by a conversion factor, plus delta-9 THC and delta-8 THC.
In other words, the state already counts the THCA that heat turns into THC, and it already counts delta-8.

The state statute bars the sale of any cannabinoid, artificially derived cannabinoid, synthetic cannabinoid "or any other product containing hemp used to aerosolize for respiratory routes of delivery, such as an inhaler, vape pen, or other device designed for such purpose."

It also bars crude extract and manufactured hemp products to which an artificially derived or synthetic cannabinoid has been added, and it limits cannabinoid-containing foods to the forms the rules allow.

The Department of Health's rules go further. No person may sell, hold for sale, offer or distribute hemp leaf, hemp floral material, "including but not limited to hemp cigars or hemp cigarettes," or viable hemp seeds, except to a USDA-licensed hemp producer or a permitted hemp processor.
The rules also bar products designed to resemble candy or to appeal to children, products that make unsubstantiated health claims, and crude extract sold directly to a consumer.

The department's registry FAQ, current as of June 23, 2026, puts the flower rule in plain words: all viable hemp seeds and hemp flower or leaf material, including hemp pre-rolls, are prohibited "regardless of the labeled percentage or amount" of THC or THCA.

blocks.x: Who must register, and who enforces

r: Act 269 of 2025, signed July 2, 2025, adds a registry for manufactured hemp product distributors and retailers. From January 1, 2026, no such distributor or retailer may sell or offer for sale without a certificate of registration.
The definition of "sale" reaches orders placed by phone, mail, catalog or the internet, and the Department of Health says out-of-state and online sellers shipping to Hawaii must register.
Carriers that only ship goods are not covered unless they sell.

The Act also creates a criminal offense. A person who is required to register, recklessly fails to, and recklessly sells or stores hemp products for sale commits unlawful hemp distribution or retailing, a misdemeanor, or a class C felony within five years of a conviction.
The penalty section of the same chapter, as the Act amends it, provides for a fine of no more than $10,000 for each separate offense.
It authorizes inspection and seizure of products and makes the offense subject to nuisance abatement.

The Department of Health and the Department of the Attorney General announced on June 23, 2026 that the grace period would end on June 30 and that enforcement of registration and existing hemp product laws would begin July 1, 2026.
The release lists fines, product embargo and seizure, and court-ordered injunctions among the tools.
Newsletters and FAQs compress. That is their job, and the compression is worth knowing about.

The Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation's March and April 2025 newsletter says the Farm Bill "defined hemp as cannabis containing no more than 0.3% THC." The Act text says delta-9 THC, which is the difference the 2025 amendment turns on.

The same newsletter says state law bans any hemp product intended for inhalation, like vape liquids and hemp flower. The vape ban sits in the statute. The flower rule sits in the department's administrative rules.

The September and October 2025 newsletter says Act 269 requires all businesses that sell hemp products to register. The Act's text covers manufactured hemp product distributors and retailers and exempts the sale of topical products and tinctures from its registration section. The department's registry FAQ lists the same exceptions, along with products that are generally recognized as safe and industrial hemp.

blocks.x: Two lines that may not match

r: The federal test and Hawaii's test already point the same direction, since both look past delta-9 to the THC that heat creates. The two differ in what they regulate. The federal definition decides what is hemp and what falls back under the Controlled Substances Act. Hawaii's rules decide what may be sold in the state, in which forms, and in what amount. Congress left room for state laws that regulate hemp production more strictly than the federal subtitle.

I cannot tell from the texts how a product that is lawful in Hawaii but outside the federal definition would be treated, or the reverse. I also cannot tell what Hawaii will do about its own calendar. The notes in the Hawaii Revised Statutes say the hemp processor chapter is repealed on July 1, 2027, and that the state's hemp definition is repealed on the same date.

items: Which federal test applies to a product on the day it is sold: the 2018 delta-9 test, or the 2025 total THC test and its exclusions?
Does a product allowed under Hawaii's rules fall inside or outside the federal definition after December 11, 2026?
Who determines "similar effects" and "container," and when?
What does a seller registered under Act 269 owe if the federal status of a product changes mid-year?
What happens on July 1, 2027, if Hawaii's hemp chapter and definitions are repealed and not replaced?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Whether Congress changes either federal date before it arrives.
How federal agencies will enforce the new definition.
The FDA lists and the "container" detail the 2025 law called for. CRS says they had not been published as of September 28, 2026.
How the federal per-container cap and Hawaii's product limits will interact for a product sold in both systems.
What Hawaii's legislature will do about the July 1, 2027 repeal dates.
The current text of USDA's hemp rule in the Code of Federal Regulations. I read the January 19, 2021 final rule and the current AMS FAQ, and I could not open the current regulation text.
Anything about a particular product or seller. This article describes law. It does not evaluate products.

posts.title: Who Sees Your Cannabis Record
posts.subtitle: A Hawaii dispensary may not be covered by HIPAA. A state rule, a registry rule and several statutes decide who sees what instead.
posts.description: What HIPAA covers, why a Hawaii cannabis dispensary may fall outside it, and which state rules decide who sees a patient record. Education, not legal advice.

r: In September 2024, Hawaii's Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation (OMCCR) told patients something that surprises many of them. Its newsletter says a medical cannabis dispensary "may not be subject to HIPAA laws." It then points to a Department of Health rule that requires every dispensary to "safeguard and keep confidential from public disclosure any personally identifying information and the medical condition" of a patient.

This article follows that sentence into the law. It is education, not legal advice. Every source is an official text or an agency page that I opened on October 11, 2026, and I report no conversation with any official, dispensary or patient. Where a source does not answer a question, I say so.
A medical cannabis patient in Hawaii leaves a trail in at least four places.

items: The certifying provider. By statute, each written certification carries the patient's name, address and patient identification number, plus other identifying information.

The Department of Health may inspect a qualifying patient's medical records held by the physician, advanced practice registered nurse or hospice provider who issued the certification, and may suspend or revoke the ability of a provider who refuses to allow it.
The Department of Health registry. Patients register with the department, and the department issues the registration certificate.
The dispensary. A retail dispensing location must require a government-issued photo identification and the department's registration card before a patient may enter.
A statewide tracking system. The department runs a computer tracking system with real time, 24-hour access to dispensary data, and each dispensary must run its own system that connects to it.

r: Each holder has a different rulebook. The rest of this article takes them in the order a patient meets them.

HIPAA is a federal law, and its rules apply to "covered entities." The regulation defines a covered entity as one of three things: a health plan, a health care clearinghouse, or "a health care provider who transmits any health information in electronic form in connection with a transaction covered by this subchapter."

A "transaction" is the transmission of information between two parties to carry out financial or administrative activities related to health care. The list includes health care claims, payment and remittance advice, claim status, enrollment in a health plan and eligibility for a health plan.

The regulation defines "health care provider" broadly. It reaches any person or organization that "furnishes, bills, or is paid for health care in the normal course of business," and its definition of "health care" includes the sale or dispensing of a drug "in accordance with a prescription."

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services puts the test plainly on its covered entity page, last modified March 16, 2026: providers who submit HIPAA transactions, like claims, electronically are covered.
The test looks at what an organization does with its data. The question is whether it sends those standard transactions electronically.

blocks.x: Why a dispensary may fall outside

r: Three Hawaii statutes point the same way. Part IX of chapter 329, the medical use of cannabis law, says it shall not be construed to require insurance coverage for the medical use of cannabis.
A separate section says the prescription requirements of section 329-38 and the pharmacy board's licensure rules do not apply to the medical use of cannabis under that part.
And no dispensary licensee, officer, employee or agent may provide written certification for the use of medical cannabis for any person.
Taken together, a dispensary sale is not insurance billing, is not a pharmacy fill under a prescription and is not a medical certification. That is the setting for OMCCR's careful word "may."
I found no source that says whether any particular Hawaii dispensary transmits standard transactions to a health plan. The newsletter itself says only that a dispensary "may" be outside HIPAA.
Whether a specific business is a covered entity depends on its own facts, and an attorney can answer that for a specific business.
A certifying provider is a different case. A certifying provider is a health care provider, and a provider's office can be a covered entity if it sends those electronic transactions.

I did not find a source on how Hawaii certifying providers handle payment for certification visits, so I leave that question open. The statute does regulate the fee a provider may charge for a certification, but it does not say how the fee is collected.

The Hawaii rule reads: "A dispensary licensee shall safeguard and keep confidential from public disclosure any personally identifying information and the medical condition of a qualifying patient or qualifying out-of-state patient."
Two details matter. The rule covers both identity and medical condition. And it is a duty on the licensee, enforced by the Department of Health.

The enforcement tools are in the same chapter. If the director finds a violation of the chapter, of chapter 329D or of a license, the director may serve a notice of violation and an order that can require the violator to stop, to pay an administrative penalty of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000 for each separate violation, and to submit a corrective action plan. Each day a violation continues counts as a separate violation. The order may also suspend or revoke a dispensary license.
The statute repeats the same fine range for violations of chapter 329D or its rules.
I read the text of the confidentiality section itself, and it contains no patient complaint procedure and no duty to tell patients if their information leaks.

Another subsection of the same section bars photography or video recording inside a dispensary facility by anyone other than the licensee, the department, law enforcement personnel or persons approved in writing by the department.

OMCCR's September 2024 newsletter describes the data flow in three sentences. OMCCR does not share a patient's specific medical information, such as qualifying conditions, with dispensaries. When a patient visits a dispensary, the 329 card registration number, name and date of birth are verified to ensure the person is a valid patient. And dispensaries have access to the total amount of cannabis the patient has purchased across all dispensaries, which helps ensure purchases stay within the allowed limit.
The newsletter adds that a patient is not required to share any medical details with dispensary staff. If the patient chooses to, the dispensary is required by law to keep those details confidential.
The totals come from law. The statute directs the tracking system to collect data on the total a patient has purchased from all retail dispensing locations in the State in any fifteen-day period.
A patient may buy from any dispensary location in the State, subject to the limits.

The rule requires each dispensary to track electronically all sales to patients from all dispensaries in the State, with a sales system that automatically blocks sales over the legal limits and cannot be overridden manually.

A visit also leaves other records. A dispensary must keep records of sales and compliance with dispensing limits for each patient, and must keep most required records at the facility for at least six years after they were prepared.
A retail dispensing location must record the name and the entry and exit date and time of every person who enters.
The statute requires video monitoring and recording on the premises, and the rules require security recordings to be kept for at least fifty days.
So one visit can create an identification check, a sales record, an entry log and video.

blocks.x: Who else can get the registry

r: The registry has its own confidentiality rule. Under HAR section 11-160-56, all information the department receives and records it keeps to run the program is confidential and not subject to disclosure, with nine exceptions.
In plain English, the exceptions are:

items: Department employees and agents who need it for official duties.
Federal, state or local law enforcement, to verify registration or for official law enforcement purposes.
A person or entity acting under a court or agency order or subpoena.
Anyone the patient authorizes in writing, with a parent, guardian or custodian signing for a minor or an adult lacking legal capacity.
Anyone a qualifying out-of-state patient authorizes in writing.
Employees or agents of the State's medical cannabis dispensary system.
Employees or agents of the department's contracted tracking software.
Dispensary licensees, as the department deems necessary to verify a person's status and to track allowable purchase limits.
Other persons the department deems necessary to administer the chapter or the dispensary system.

r: The rule adds that the department may notify law enforcement about falsified or fraudulent information, notify state or local law enforcement about suspected crimes, and publish non-identifying aggregated data.
The rule cites the public records law, HRS section 92F-13, among the provisions it implements.

The statute is consistent. When a law enforcement agency inquires, at any hour, the department must immediately verify whether the subject has registered and may provide reasonable access to the registry information for official law enforcement purposes.

A separate statute reaches the dispensaries. Section 329D-20 says that, notwithstanding any other law, the department shall disclose information, documents and other records regarding medical cannabis dispensaries and production centers, on request, to any state, federal or county agency engaged in the criminal investigation or prosecution of violations of laws related to the operations or activities of a dispensary.

The section speaks of records regarding dispensaries and production centers. It does not say whether patient-level sales records fall inside that phrase, and a different section defines "medical cannabis dispensary records" only for its own offense of falsifying them.
I found nothing that settles the question.

Hawaii's Constitution recognizes a right of privacy: "The right of the people to privacy is recognized and shall not be infringed without the showing of a compelling state interest. The legislature shall take affirmative steps to implement this right."
I did not research how courts apply that clause to a private business, so I cite it only as the constitutional backdrop.

The Uniform Information Practices Act, chapter 92F, is a public records law for government agencies. It does not require disclosure of government records that would be a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, and it lists information relating to medical history, diagnosis, condition, treatment or evaluation as an example of information in which a person has a significant privacy interest.
That helps explain the registry's confidentiality rule. I found nothing in the sources that makes the act apply to a dispensary's own files.

Hawaii's security breach statute, chapter 487N, requires a business that owns or licenses personal information of Hawaii residents, and a government agency that collects personal information for specific government purposes, to notify affected people of a security breach without unreasonable delay.

The statute defines "personal information" as a first name or initial and last name combined with a Social Security number, a driver's license or Hawaii identification card number, or an account, credit or debit card number with an access code that would permit access to a financial account.

A medical condition, a 329 card number and a purchase history are not on that list. A leak of a list that held names and medical conditions but none of those listed data elements would not match the statute's definition, as I read it. Dispensaries check a government-issued photo identification at the door, and I do not know whether any dispensary keeps the identification number.

On April 28, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice published a final rule, effective that day, placing FDA-approved drug products containing marijuana, and marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license, in schedule III. The rule also creates an expedited DEA registration pathway for entities that hold state medical marijuana licenses, as manufacturers, distributors or dispensers.

Federal registrants must keep records and submit reports. The rule says reporting and recordkeeping are limited to what federal statute and treaty obligations require, and that state-required records are accepted to the maximum extent permissible. It also says a state-authorized certification can support dispensing if it includes the user's name and address, is dated and signed on the day it is issued, and identifies the issuing practitioner.

I found no mention of HIPAA or patient privacy in the text I read. Federal registration and HIPAA coverage are separate questions. HIPAA coverage turns on being a health plan, a clearinghouse or a provider that sends standard transactions.
The Federal Register notice does not address whether registration changes that, so I note the gap and leave the question open. I also did not find whether any Hawaii dispensary has registered.

items: You are not required to share medical details with dispensary staff.
If you do share them, the dispensary must keep them confidential.
A visit involves an identification check, a card number, purchase totals, an entry log and video.
The registry's nine exceptions are public text. You can read them in HAR section 11-160-56.
The dispensary rules are on OMCCR's Laws and Rules page. OMCCR lists the dispensary chapter, 11-850, as interim rules effective December 6, 2024.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Whether any Hawaii dispensary or certifying provider is a HIPAA covered entity. The newsletter says only "may not," and I found nothing on billing. The HHS guidance pages on hhs.gov returned HTTP 403 to my requests, so I did not open them. I relied on the regulation and on CMS.
How the Department of Health enforces section 11-850-40, or how many complaints it has received. I found no data.
Whether section 329D-20 reaches patient-level sales records.

Whether Hawaii has a general consumer privacy statute beyond the ones cited here. I did not search 2026 session laws, and the Hawaii Revised Statutes pages I opened were posted in January 2026 and may not reflect later acts.
What a dispensary keeps about a patient beyond what the rules list, including whether it stores identification numbers.
Whether the interim dispensary rules have been amended since December 2024. OMCCR's page says Act 46 of 2025 extended the interim rules' sunset date by two years.
I did not look for later amendments.
What the April 2026 federal rule means for patient data in Hawaii.

r: This article is education, not legal advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney.

posts.title: No Organic Seal for Cannabis
posts.subtitle: Hawaii lets a dispensary use the word organic only if USDA permits it. Here is what that rule, federal law and the April 2026 rescheduling order say about why cannabis has no organic seal, and what might change.
posts.description: Why Hawaii cannabis cannot be labeled organic, what USDA says about hemp, what federal law says about marijuana, and what the April 2026 rescheduling order does and does not change. Education, not legal advice.

r: Hawaii's dispensary labeling rule contains one sentence about the word organic: "A dispensary licensee shall not label as organic any cannabis or manufactured cannabis product unless permitted by the United States Department of Agriculture in accordance with the Organic Foods Production Act."
The state does not run its own organic program for cannabis. It points to Washington, D.C.

A public training deck hosted by OMCCR says the same thing in plainer words. A slide in the Know Before You Grow deck, which OMCCR hosted in Kona on March 7, 2026, shows the USDA organic seal and the caption: "Federal Cert, but cannabis is still federally illegal (no cert)."

The deck carries a disclaimer that the views expressed in the webinar do not necessarily reflect the opinions or policies of the State of Hawaii or the Department of Health, so I cite the slide as a public statement of what was presented, not as agency policy.

This article follows that caption into the law. It is education, not legal advice. Every source is an official text or an agency page that I opened on October 11, 2026, and I report no conversation with any official. Where a source does not answer a question, I say so.

Congress told the Secretary of Agriculture to establish an organic certification program for producers and handlers of agricultural products "that have been produced using organic methods as provided for in this chapter."
The rules are in 7 CFR part 205. They define "organic" as "a labeling term that refers to an agricultural product produced in accordance with the Act and the regulations in this part."

The core rule is about who must be certified. Each operation, or part of an operation, that produces or handles agricultural products "intended to be sold, labeled, or represented as '100 percent organic,' 'organic,' or 'made with organic'" must be certified, except for exempt operations.
Anyone who knowingly sells or labels a product as organic outside the Act faces a civil penalty.

There is a small-seller exemption: an operation whose gross income from organic sales is $5,000 or less a year does not need certification, but it must still follow the production and labeling requirements.
The statute has the Secretary carry out the program through certifying agents.

The rules also give residue testing a role. If testing detects prohibited substances at levels greater than 5 percent of the Environmental Protection Agency's tolerance for the specific residue detected, or unavoidable residual environmental contamination, the product must not be sold or labeled as organic.

blocks.x: The first test is a definition

r: Both the statute and the regulation define "agricultural product" as "any agricultural commodity or product, whether raw or processed, including any commodity or product derived from livestock," that is "marketed in the United States for human or livestock consumption."
I did not find a source that applies that phrase to cannabis, so I treat it only as the starting point of the program: a product has to be an agricultural product before it can be certified at all.

USDA does say hemp can be certified. The National Organic Program's instruction on organic certification of industrial hemp production, NOP 2040 Revision 04, is dated November 26, 2019. It says that for hemp produced in the United States, "only hemp produced in accordance with the U.S. Domestic Hemp Production Program and/or the 2014 Farm Bill may be certified as organic, if produced in accordance with USDA organic regulations."
The Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) hemp FAQ repeats it in a question and answer: hemp produced in the U.S. under the Domestic Hemp Production Program may be certified as organic.
The program handbook's index lists the instruction under the same date.

The same FAQ draws the line between hemp and marijuana. It says the legal difference is the amount of THC the plant contains, that a cannabis plant with more than 0.3 percent THC is considered marijuana, and that "You cannot produce medical or recreational marijuana with a hemp license."

The Controlled Substances Act says the same thing in statutory terms: it defines marijuana as all parts of the plant Cannabis sativa L., and then provides that the term does not include hemp as defined in 7 U.S.C. 1639o.
The April 2026 rule notes that the hemp definition is being amended, effective November 12, 2026, to refer to total tetrahydrocannabinols.
I did not read the amendment itself, so I stop at that note.

blocks.x: What federal law says about marijuana

r: Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act lists marihuana, and it lists tetrahydrocannabinols "except for tetrahydrocannabinols in hemp."
That is the statute on the books in the 2024 edition of the U.S. Code that I opened.

On April 28, 2026, the Department of Justice published a final rule that changed part of the picture. It places FDA-approved drug products containing marijuana, and marijuana "subject to a state-issued license to manufacture, distribute, and/or dispense marijuana or products containing marijuana for medical purposes," in schedule III. It took effect that day.

The rule is explicit about what it leaves alone. Any form of marijuana other than an FDA-approved drug product or marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license "remains a schedule I controlled substance."
It does not apply to synthetically derived THC, and it does not affect the status of hemp.

The Department of Justice published a second notice the same day, announcing a hearing on the broader proposal to move marijuana from schedule I to schedule III. The notice set the hearing for June 29, 2026, to conclude no later than July 15.

A law firm's client alert dated September 24, 2026, reports that the hearing concluded and that the parties await a recommended decision from the administrative law judge and a later final determination by the DEA administrator.
That alert is a secondary source. I did not find the outcome in an official document.

blocks.x: What Hawaii's rule does with all that

r: The Hawaii rule sits in the packaging and labeling section of the dispensary chapter. It borrows the federal test instead of writing its own. A dispensary can label a product organic only where USDA permits it under the Organic Foods Production Act.
That puts the decision with USDA, not with the Department of Health.

The state's statute shows the word is not foreign to its own program. When the Department of Health sets standards for laboratory testing, the statute says that for microbiological impurities the department shall consider "the benefits of organically grown cannabis that features the use of bacteria in lieu of pesticides."

And OMCCR's patient education uses the word as a growing method. Its October 2024 newsletter says: "Use organic nutrients and pesticides, whenever possible, to minimize toxic chemicals in your medical cannabis."

Its December 2024 newsletter says to use organic methods and a pest schedule that works for your environment, and lists neem oil sprays, organic insecticidal soap, organic soil top dressings and ladybugs as natural pest control.
Both uses can be true at once. Growing with organic methods is a practice. The organic seal is a federal certification, and the deck slide says the certification is unavailable for cannabis.
A patient growing at home is not selling or labeling a product, and the rule I read governs dispensary licensees.
I did not find a source that says how the labeling rule applies to anyone else.

blocks.x: How California handled the same wall

r: California took a different route. Its Department of Food and Agriculture runs the OCal program, a statewide certification for "comparable-to-organic" cannabis. The department's page explains the name: "only the National Organic Program can authorize use of the word 'organic' on product packaging," and "Since cannabis is illegal under federal law, cannabis products are not eligible to carry the 'organic' designation."
Cultivators and distributors certified by a registered certifying agent may sell or label products as OCal. Licensed manufacturers are certified by the California Department of Public Health instead.
The page says the Office of Administrative Law approved the OCal regulations and that the program is currently accepting applications for registration and accreditation of certifying agents.
A department flyer, a PDF created in February 2021, describes the program the same way: standards "comparable to the National Organic Program."
I opened no Hawaii counterpart. The sources I opened show a Hawaii rule that defers to USDA and no Hawaii program that certifies comparable-to-organic cannabis.
Three questions sit inside the phrase "what rescheduling might change."
First, does Schedule III end the federal problem? The April order places the covered products in schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act, which is still a schedule of controlled substances.
The same order requires DEA registration for those who handle them, and it keeps unlicensed marijuana in schedule I.
The law firm alert adds that even if the broader proposal is finalized, marijuana would remain a federally controlled substance subject to applicable requirements.

Second, does USDA's program turn on scheduling status? The statements I found tie the lack of an organic path to federal illegality. The deck's slide says "still federally illegal (no cert)," and California's agriculture department says cannabis products are not eligible because cannabis is illegal under federal law.
I found no USDA document that states the test for marijuana in its own words, and no USDA or AMS statement about the April 2026 order. USDA's published pathway covers hemp.
Third, who would decide? Under Hawaii's rule, USDA, not the Department of Health.
If USDA ever opened a path, the Hawaii rule would not need to change for a dispensary to use it. If USDA does not, the rule keeps the word off dispensary labels.
One more limit matters. The April order's covered category is marijuana subject to a state-issued license to manufacture, distribute or dispense.
Hawaii's dispensary licenses fit that wording on its face. I did not find whether the order reaches Hawaii patient or caregiver registrations, which are a different kind of authorization.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Any USDA or AMS statement about marijuana in its own words. The statements I found are on a slide in a deck that OMCCR hosted and on a California Department of Food and Agriculture page, and a USDA instruction and FAQ about hemp.
Whether USDA has said anything about organic eligibility since the April 2026 order. I found nothing.
The outcome of the DEA hearing on the broader proposal. The only account I found is a law firm's alert dated September 24, 2026.
How the Hawaii labeling rule applies to anyone other than a dispensary licensee.
Whether the interim dispensary rules have been amended since December 2024. The version I opened was effective December 6, 2024.
Whether Hawaii will create a comparable-to-organic program like California's. I found no sign of one.
Anything that has happened since October 11, 2026.

r: This article is education, not legal advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney.

posts.title: Inhaled Residue
posts.subtitle: Hawaii tests dispensary cannabis against a 56-entry pesticide list. Food follows a different rulebook, and the sources I opened show where the two diverge.
posts.description: How Hawaii tests dispensary cannabis for pesticides, how federal food tolerances differ, what EPA and the Hawaii Department of Agriculture have said about cannabis, and what the record does not show. Education, not legal or medical advice.

r: Hawaii's dispensary rules set one number for pesticides. Section 11-850-135 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules says a laboratory's certificate of analysis must show the presence of "Pesticides listed in Table 4, each with a limit of 1.0 parts per million (ppm)." Table 4 has 56 entries.
A batch over any limit cannot be dispensed.

Food does not work that way. For food, the federal government sets a separate maximum for each pesticide on each food. Whether and how that framework applies to a product that is smoked or vaporized is the open question this article follows. It lays the two systems side by side and says where the sources stop. It is education, not legal or medical advice. Every source is an official text or an agency page that I opened on October 11, 2026, and I report no conversation with any official.

Federal law says a pesticide residue in or on a food "shall be deemed unsafe" unless a tolerance is in effect and the residue is within its limits, or an exemption from the requirement of a tolerance is in effect.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) describes the tolerance as "the maximum amount of a pesticide allowed to remain in or on a food," and its public page is headed "Pesticides Have Different Tolerances for Different Foods."

EPA's registration manual adds the enforcement side. A tolerance is the maximum residue level of a pesticide, usually measured in parts per million, that legally can be present in food or feed. If residues exceed the tolerance, or no tolerance has been established, the crop is considered adulterated and may be seized by the Food and Drug Administration, the Department of Agriculture or a state enforcement agency.

The statute also sets the safety standard. EPA may establish or leave in effect a tolerance only if it determines the tolerance is safe, and "safe" means a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure to the residue, "including all anticipated dietary exposures and all other exposures for which there is reliable information."
The statute names dietary exposure first and then "all other exposures for which there is reliable information."
A second federal rule sits beside it. It is unlawful to use a registered pesticide in a manner inconsistent with its labeling.
The label is where a pesticide's permitted crops and methods are written down.

blocks.x: What EPA has said about cannabis

r: At a November 1, 2017, meeting of its Pesticide Program Dialogue Committee, EPA presented a cannabis status update. It said there were no pesticides registered by EPA specifically for use on marijuana, though some pesticide labels list industrial hemp among their crops. It said there were no tolerances established for marijuana or hemp, and that cannabis did not fit into an existing crop group. It also said pesticides exempt from federal registration under section 25(b) of the federal pesticide law are not prohibited from use on cannabis.

The same presentation reports that in spring 2017 four states each issued four special local need registrations for tolerance-exempt products for use on cannabis, that EPA notified the states of its intent to disapprove them, and that three states withdrew theirs while EPA disapproved Nevada's. It adds that some states had established their own pesticide residue action levels for cannabis, and that SFIREG had raised concerns about them.
Hawaii's Table 4 is a state-set residue limit of the kind the slide describes. The slide did not name Hawaii and predates the interim rules I read, so I do not read it as a statement about them.

A 2015 EPA letter to the Colorado Department of Agriculture explains how EPA thought about cannabis exposure. EPA encouraged states to pursue special local need registrations only where a federally registered pesticide has similar use patterns. The letter lists what it would look for: approval for use on food, to have a complete toxicity database; approval for use on tobacco, "in order to have a pyrolysis study to determine the breakdown products formed when the treated plant material is burned"; the same application methods; crops with agronomic characteristics similar to cannabis; and the same kind of structure or site.
EPA's letter ties the tobacco criterion to what happens when treated plant material is burned.

The picture has not stood still for hemp. On April 13, 2023, EPA announced its first pesticide tolerance for hemp, for the herbicide ethalfluralin, on hemp seed. EPA noted that biopesticides already registered for use on hemp are tolerance-exempt.
That is a tolerance for a seed. I found no tolerance for cannabis flower.

The Hawaii Department of Agriculture's Pesticides Branch posted "Criteria for Pesticides Used in the Production of Medical Marijuana in the State of Hawaii" in January 2017. It says there were then "no products registered for use on marijuana, either with the United States Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) or with the Hawaii State Department of Agriculture (HDOA)." A product could still be used in marijuana production if it met all of three requirements. It must be either EPA registered and licensed by the department, or a minimum risk pesticide exempt from federal registration. The active ingredients on its label must be exempt from the requirement of a tolerance on all food crops. And the label's directions and restrictions must be general enough to allow use on marijuana.

The guidance adds a route for products that fail those tests, a special local need registration under the federal pesticide law, and sets minimum requirements for it. Two of them track EPA's 2015 letter: the product must be registered for use on food, and its active ingredient must have an existing tolerance for use on tobacco.
The guidance says the requirements "may be changed at any time."

The Pesticides Branch page, which I opened on October 11, 2026, still links to a document titled "Guidance on Pesticide Use on Medical Marijuana" and dated January 2017. The department's site now uses the name Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity.
I found no newer version. The same page carries a notice that as of January 1, 2023, all uses and sale of chlorpyrifos are banned in Hawaii.

The statute that created the dispensary system tells the Department of Health to establish and enforce laboratory-based testing standards for content, contamination and consistency. When it does, it must "review and take guidance from the testing programs and standards for pesticides under the regulations of the United States Environmental Protection Agency," and consider processes that may allow batches that fail to be remediated.

The rule turns that into a procedure. A dispensary may not dispense cannabis unless a laboratory certified by the department has analyzed a representative sample and the sample meets the subchapter's requirements.
The laboratory issues a certificate of analysis to the dispensary and the department for each batch.
The certificate must show the heavy metals in Table 3, the pesticides in Table 4 at 1.0 ppm each, microbial contaminants, mycotoxins, foreign material and water activity.
If a limit is exceeded, the dispensary shall not dispense any portion of the batch that does not conform.

Here is where the pesticide limit differs from the other limits. The rule lets a dispensary remediate some failures, with a plan filed with the department and a retest. The list of what may be remediated names heavy metals, foreign or extraneous material, microbial contaminants, mycotoxins and water activity. For manufactured products it adds solvents and dosage limits.
Pesticides are not on the list. A non-conforming batch must be disposed of or destroyed under video camera surveillance within thirty days, and it stays in quarantine until any reanalysis is done.

The enforcement tools are in the same chapter. The director may serve a notice of violation and an order that can require a violator to stop, pay a penalty of $100 to $1,000 for each separate violation, and submit a corrective action plan, and may suspend or revoke a license.
Two features set the rule apart from food tolerances. It uses one limit for all 56 entries, where EPA says tolerances differ by pesticide and by food.
And it tests the finished batch, where the federal system describes a maximum amount allowed to remain on a food after the pesticide has been used under a label.

OMCCR's July 2024 newsletter explains how to read a certificate of analysis. Next to the pesticide section, it says: "All pesticides that are tested are listed. For testing rules and regulations, see Hawai'i administrative rules 11-850-135."

For growers, OMCCR's public education says three things. The December 2024 newsletter says to avoid spraying flower buds with pesticides, even organic ones, because residues left behind can be harmful when inhaled, and that if you do spray, it is crucial to wash your flower buds after harvesting.

The October 2024 newsletter says cannabis is a bio-accumulator, meaning the plant can absorb heavy metals and toxins, such as pesticides used years ago, and advises testing soil before planting directly in the ground.

A public Know Before You Grow deck that OMCCR hosted in Kona repeats the pest management and the soil advice. It carries a disclaimer that the views expressed do not necessarily reflect the policies of the State or the Department of Health.

A common line is that cannabis is a plant you cannot wash. OMCCR's own text points the other way: wash buds after harvest if you sprayed. I did not find a source that measures how much residue washing removes from cannabis flower, so I do not make a claim in either direction.

The dispensary rule governs dispensary batches. The statute has one more line for patients and caregivers. The department's testing standards must "include permission for qualifying patients and primary caregivers to obtain testing services directly from certified laboratories on the island where the qualifying patient and primary caregiver reside."
I did not find a source that shows which certified laboratories offer that service, or at what price.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: How much pesticide residue on cannabis flower reaches the lungs when it is smoked or vaporized. EPA's 2015 letter treats burning as a reason to ask for a pyrolysis study, but I did not open any measurement.
Whether Hawaii's 1.0 ppm limit is a health threshold. The rule states the number. I found no document in the sources I opened that explains how it was chosen.
Whether EPA has changed its position on cannabis since November 1, 2017. I found its April 2023 tolerance for hemp seed and nothing for cannabis flower.
Whether the January 2017 Hawaii Department of Agriculture guidance has been updated. It is still posted, and I found no newer version.
How much washing removes residue from cannabis flower.
Whether the interim dispensary rules have been amended since December 2024. The version I opened was effective December 6, 2024.
Anything that has happened since October 11, 2026.

r: This article is education, not legal or medical advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney, and for health questions, ask your clinician.

posts.title: The Lab Rules
posts.subtitle: How Hawaii's testing rules for medical cannabis moved from counts of microbes to a list of named organisms, and what it means that one lab is certified today.
posts.description: How Hawaii's medical cannabis lab rule moved from microbe counts to six named organisms between 2015 and 2025, and what one certified lab means. Education, not legal advice.

r: A certificate of analysis for a product from a Hawaii dispensary has a box for microbials. The Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation (OMCCR) explained that box in its July 2024 newsletter: the contaminants listed there must not be detected in one gram of the cannabis or manufactured cannabis product.

That sentence describes the rule as it stands. It does not describe the rule Hawaii started with. In 2015 the first dispensary rules set count limits for four broad groups of microbes and added a short list of named organisms on top. Since February 24, 2022 the rule has been a list of named organisms only. This article follows the change, version by version, using the Department of Health's own posted texts. It is education, not legal advice. Every source was opened on October 11, 2026. None comes from a conversation with an official, a lab or a grower.

Hawaii Revised Statutes section 329D-8 tells the Department to set and enforce standards for lab-based testing of cannabis and manufactured cannabis products, for content, contamination and consistency. While setting those standards, the Department must review other jurisdictions' testing programs, consider the effect of the standards on the retail cost to the qualifying patient, and consider processes that would allow a batch that fails to be remediated. For microbiological impurities it must consider the benefits of organically grown cannabis that uses bacteria in place of pesticides.
The same section says the Department may certify laboratories, and that a dispensary whose batch fails may have the batch retested, at its own expense, by the same lab or a different one.
The Department's dispensary program page describes its oversight as statewide, covering the labs that test the safety and quality of the products.
The statute names no organisms and sets no limits. That work sits in the administrative rules.

blocks.x: 2015: counts, plus a short named list

r: The first dispensary rules, chapter 11-850 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules, took effect on December 14, 2015. Section 11-850-85, later renumbered 11-850-135, told a certified lab what each certificate of analysis had to show.

For microbes, the section listed "microbiological impurities, including but not limited to" four groups with count limits: total viable aerobic bacteria, total yeast and mold, total coliforms, and bile-tolerant gram-negative bacteria. Each group had one limit for unprocessed and processed plant material and a lower one for CO2 and solvent-based extracts.

Two further lines worked differently. Pathogenic strains of E. coli and Salmonella had to be not detected in one gram. Three Aspergillus species, A. fumigatus, A. flavus and A. niger, had a limit of less than one colony-forming unit per gram.
The same section capped the moisture content of plant material at under 15 percent.
A count limit says how much of a group is allowed. A not-detected line says whether a named organism turns up at all. The 2015 rule used both.

blocks.x: February 24, 2022: the count limits come out

r: On February 24, 2022 the Department put amended interim rules into effect.

The Department posts a Ramseyer version of that text. Ramseyer format shows deleted wording in brackets and new wording without them, so a reader can see exactly what changed. In the testing section, all four count groups sit inside the deletion brackets. The words "pathogenic strains" are bracketed out of the E. coli line, and the "less than one colony-forming unit" wording is bracketed out of the Aspergillus line.

What takes their place is one lead-in: "The following microbial contaminants, which must not be detected in one gram of cannabis or manufactured cannabis product." The list under it names E. coli, Salmonella, and four Aspergillus species. The fourth, A. terreus, is new.

The Department's executive summary of the 2022 changes gives two lines to this. Under testing it lists "Revised microbial contaminants list; allow non-plating methods," and "Change from moisture content to water activity (for cannabis)."

The summary does not define "non-plating methods." Plating is the traditional way of counting microbes by growing them on a culture dish, so the phrase suggests the Department opened the door to other kinds of test. That is my reading. The summary says no more, and I found no document that explains the choice.
The water rule changed in the same step. Cannabis flower now had a water activity limit of 0.65 in place of a moisture percentage.
OMCCR's July 2024 newsletter describes water activity as a measure shown on the certificate, and says safe moisture levels "help to prevent undesirable microorganisms from growing."

blocks.x: 2022: one organism in, out and in again

r: The list moved twice more that year. The February text included Aspergillus terreus. The Department's summary of the amendments effective April 29, 2022 says to remove it, and the April 29 Ramseyer version shows it in deletion brackets.
The same summary changed the water rule to read "water activity (aw), which shall not exceed 0.65; or moisture content, which shall not exceed fifteen per cent."

The Department's list of amendments effective November 17, 2022 then adds Aspergillus terreus back, removes the "or moisture content" option so that water activity stands alone, and adds a water activity limit for kief and hashish.
Neither list gives a reason for the removal or the return.

The November 2022 amendments also changed how a failed batch is handled. The Department's summary says they "expand possibilities and codify procedures for remediation of batches failing testing standards."

blocks.x: What has stayed the same since

r: The six-organism list appears in the Ramseyer versions effective August 7, 2023 and December 6, 2024, and in the compiled chapter that took effect on November 17, 2025.

In the current text, section 11-850-135 points to a table of microbial contaminants in Appendix I: E. coli, Salmonella, A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. niger and A. terreus, each of which "must not be detected in one gram." Mycotoxins sit in a separate table.

Here is the sequence of versions the Department posts on its chapter 11-850 page: December 14, 2015; February 24, 2022; April 29, 2022; November 17, 2022; August 7, 2023; April 5, 2024; December 6, 2024; and November 17, 2025.
I read the text or the Department's summary of each version except April 5, 2024.

The chapter is still labeled interim rules. Act 46 of 2025 moved the end date for the Department's interim dispensary rules to July 1, 2027, or until final rules are adopted under the standard rulemaking chapter, whichever comes first.

blocks.x: A failed batch can come back

r: Under the current rules a batch that exceeds a limit may not be dispensed.

Microbial contaminants are on the short list of problems that may be remediated. The dispensary must send the Department a remediation plan, with evidence that the method works, within 30 days of the certificate of analysis. It may start only after the Department approves the plan. The batch must then be reanalyzed by a certified lab, and nothing from it may be distributed until the Department approves. If the reanalysis fails, or the plan is not approved, the batch is disposed of. Mixing a failing batch into another one makes the whole mixture deemed contaminated, whatever the later results say.
A batch that cannot be sold or remediated has to be disposed of under video camera surveillance within thirty days, and a non-conforming batch must be quarantined until any reanalysis is finished.
The statute asked the Department to consider remediation processes.
The rule is how it did.
A dispensary may not dispense cannabis unless a laboratory certified by the Department has analyzed a representative sample and the sample meets the rule's requirements.
OMCCR's page of certified cannabis testing facilities lists one: Spectra Analytical Lab.

The July 2024 newsletter said the same, in a footnote to the certificate guide: that lab was "currently the only DOH-certified cannabis testing lab in the state," and a certificate from any other lab means the product is not a Hawaii-licensed product.

It has not always been one lab. A Department news release dated July 31, 2017 announced the first provisional certification, for Steep Hill Hawaii, a private lab on Oahu, and said the State Laboratories Division was working with two other private labs.

The Department's December 2017 update reports that Pharmlab Hawaii became the first private lab on Maui to get the go-ahead in October 2017, and that a third private lab was preparing for an onsite inspection.
The current list shows one lab. I found no document that says why the others are not on it.

blocks.x: What it takes to be certified

r: The 2017 release said a lab seeking certification had to submit validation studies for each testing area, among them microbial contaminants, "intestinal bacteria and pathogens," dangerous molds and the toxins molds produce, and had to meet ISO accreditation standards.

The Department's testing facility application, posted in August 2026, shows the present version of that process. A lab checks the areas it wants to be certified for. The microbiology section has six boxes, the same six organisms: E. coli, Salmonella species, and four Aspergillus species. A second section asks whether the lab is ISO 17025 accredited, whether its parent company is, or whether it has applied, and says that having applied is the minimum requirement.

blocks.x: Reading a certificate with this in mind

r: OMCCR's guide to the certificate says "ND" means not detected, and that the contaminants in the microbial section must not be detected in one gram.
So for those six organisms, "not detected" is the passing result.

A list of named organisms tells you what the lab looked for. I found nothing in the Department's texts that says a product is free of every microbe, and a reader should not take the list to say so. The rules also govern what dispensaries sell. The statute separately tells the Department to let qualifying patients and caregivers get testing services directly from certified labs on the island where they live.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Why the Department changed the microbial list in 2022. The summaries I read give the change and no reason.
Why Aspergillus terreus was removed in April 2022 and restored in November 2022.
Why one lab is certified now, and what became of the labs certified in 2017.
How labs run the tests, how often batches fail, or how often they are remediated. I found no Department data on this.
Whether final rules will replace the interim rules by July 1, 2027.
Any lab's results for any product.
The full text of the November 17, 2022 and April 5, 2024 versions. I read the Department's summaries of them.

r: This article is education, not legal advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney.

posts.title: Why Report
posts.subtitle: After a bad reaction to a cannabis or hemp product, Hawaii has one route for the emergency and one for the record. Here is how each works, what dispensaries must do, and what the public record leaves out.
posts.description: Hawaii's two routes after a bad reaction to a cannabis or hemp product: 911 and the Poison Center, then OMCCR's forms; what dispensaries must report; what the record does not show. Education, not legal or medical advice.

r: The Office of Medical Cannabis Control and Regulation (OMCCR) keeps a page for people who have had a bad reaction. It opens with a line for emergencies: contact 911. It then says that anyone experiencing an unwanted reaction or adverse effect because of medical cannabis or a hemp product should contact the Hawaiʻi Poison Center at 1-800-222-1222. Once the person has recovered, OMCCR asks them to follow up by submitting a form, and says staff will get back to them.

This article walks through that route and the rules behind it. It is education, not legal or medical advice. If you or someone near you is in danger, call 911 first. Every source below was opened on October 11, 2026. None comes from a conversation with an official, a patient or a dispensary.
The order on OMCCR's page matters. The emergency line comes first, the Poison Center second and the OMCCR form last, and the form is meant for "once you have recovered."
The Poison Center page describes a service that is open 24 hours a day, every day, free, and "100% confidential," staffed by trained nurses, pharmacists and physician toxicologists.
The same page shows totals for 2023, updated February 20, 2024: 5,960 exposure cases of all kinds, 89.3 percent of them managed at home.
Those figures cover every kind of poisoning. They say nothing about cannabis alone.

The OMCCR form asks how the office may contact you, by email, by phone or both, and requires at least one. A name is optional. The one required field is a detailed description of the incident, the adverse event, or the issues behind a complaint. The page promises that OMCCR will keep your information confidential.

Read side by side, OMCCR's pages suggest a simple split. If your body reacted, the Poison Center is for advice now, and the adverse event form is the follow-up once you have recovered. If something about the product itself looks wrong, the product complaint form takes a description and photos.
The two can describe the same event, and nothing on the pages says you may not file both. That is my reading of the pages, and OMCCR has not said it in those words.

blocks.x: A second form, for the product

r: OMCCR runs a separate "File a Product Complaint" form. It asks for a name, email address or phone number if you want to be contacted, all optional, and a detailed description, which is required. It accepts up to 10 attached files, up to 100 MB each.
The dispensary program page links the same form.

OMCCR's hemp program FAQ, current as of December 16, 2025, says a person filing a product complaint may stay anonymous or give contact information that "will remain confidential," and that the adverse event form, by contrast, needs accurate contact information.

The two forms overlap on purpose. The dispensary rules define a product complaint as any communication that expresses concern with the quality of cannabis or a manufactured cannabis product "for any reason." Their list of examples includes foul odor, off taste, mislabeling, foreign material in a container, and "illness or injury."
An adverse reaction can be both an event that happened to a person and a complaint about a product.
The adverse event page says "medical cannabis or hemp product."

OMCCR's hemp program links both forms from its home page, and its consumer FAQ answers the question directly. A person who believes a hemp product caused an adverse event can use the adverse event form. The FAQ adds a note: OMCCR does not provide medical advice, and anyone having a medical event after using a hemp or cannabis product, or a parent whose child is, should seek medical attention immediately.
OMCCR's home page says the office administers three programs: the patient registry, the dispensary program and the hemp program.
One pair of forms serves all three.

The reporting duty in the rules sits on dispensaries. Section 11-850-126 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules requires each dispensary to follow written procedures and to notify the Department of Health within 48 hours after learning of an adverse event associated with cannabis or a manufactured cannabis product sold at one of its retail locations. The rule defines an adverse event as "any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of cannabis or a manufactured cannabis product, which may include any unfavorable or unintended sign, symptom, or disease."

Section 11-850-125 covers product complaints. A qualified person at the dispensary must review every complaint to decide whether it involves a possible failure to meet the contaminant limits or any other requirement whose failure may risk illness or injury, and must investigate each one that does. Quality control staff approve the decision to investigate and the findings, and the work extends to all relevant batches and records.

Put the rules together and a complaint inside a dispensary follows a path. The complaint is recorded. A qualified person reviews it for a possible failure to meet a limit or another requirement. If there is one, it is investigated, with quality control approving the decision and the findings, across the relevant batches. An adverse event goes to the Department within 48 hours. If the product has to come off the shelf, a recall starts, and the Department hears within 24 hours. A batch that fails a testing limit may be remediated and reanalyzed with the Department's approval, or disposed of.

Section 11-850-127 covers recalls. A dispensary must have a written recall plan, must notify the Department in writing within 24 hours of starting a recall, and must warn patients and the public about a hazard when that is appropriate to protect public health.

Section 11-850-128 sets out what a dispensary records. For a product complaint tied to production practices, the record includes the product's name and description, the batch number if available, the date and the complainant's contact details if available, the nature of the complaint "including, if known, how the cannabis or manufactured cannabis product was used," the reply and the findings. The dispensary also keeps a written record of every adverse event and every report of one to the Department.
The Department's executive summary of the February 2022 rule changes lists "Adverse event reporting" among the new safety measures for all products.
The sections carry an effective date of February 24, 2022.
I found no rule that requires a patient or caregiver to report. The duty in the texts I read falls on the license holder. A patient's report is voluntary.

blocks.x: What a report can set off

r: The record shows two examples of OMCCR acting on concerns it received.

On April 19, 2023, OMCCR sent registered patients a short notice titled "Adverse Event Investigation." It said the office had received complaints of adverse reactions to cannabis products, and that the Department of Health's Disease Outbreak Control Division, Disease Investigation Branch, was contacting people registered in the program to find out whether they had experienced an adverse reaction.
The notice does not say which products, how many complaints, or what the investigation found.

On February 2, 2023, OMCCR issued a patient advisory after receiving "inquiries raising concerns" about an event held at a farm that is not a licensed dispensary. It told registered patients that using products distributed there was outside the scope of lawful medical use and might not be safe, and said no product distributed at the event was legally regulated or subject to testing for solvents, pesticides, heavy metals or other contamination.
The advisory names the event and the farm. I leave both out, because the point here is the pattern. A concern reached the office, and the office told the public.
OMCCR's advisories page lists both documents, with a third item, the executive order guidance on caregivers.
The record I opened does not link the two documents to each other. They show that reports and inquiries can reach OMCCR, and that OMCCR has, at least twice, answered them in public.

A form is only as useful as the office reading it. OMCCR's January 20, 2026 annual report to the Legislature says the program's current staffing is inadequate for the growing number of facilities, the added complexity of its processes and its hemp duties. It asks for at least two compliance officers, one data scientist, one program planner and one accountant, and says the rise in cannabinoid hemp and unlicensed retailers has increased the need for oversight.

The governor's executive order guidance from December 2024 says the same thing from another side: it states that OMCCR has limited resources to investigate and enforce minor violations of the caregiver part of the law.
Neither document is about adverse event reports. Both are the office describing its own capacity in public, and a reader deciding how to use the forms should have that context.

blocks.x: Why this matters for what is not regulated

r: A product from a licensed dispensary comes with batch records, a certificate of analysis from a certified lab and a recall plan. A complaint about it leads, by rule, to a review of the batch.
Products from outside the dispensary system have none of that. The 2023 advisory said so about one event.
That leaves a patient's own report as the main way a problem with such a product can reach anyone. This is my reading of the record, and I did not find OMCCR or the Poison Center saying it.

blocks.x: What to include in a report

r: OMCCR's forms ask for a description. The dispensary rule on complaint records shows what the office's licensees are expected to capture: what the product was, the batch number if there is one, the date, how the product was used, and what happened.
If you are filing a report, those are sensible things to have ready. This is a suggestion drawn from the rule, not a Hawaii requirement.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: How many reports OMCCR or the Poison Center receive, how many concern cannabis or hemp, or what changes follow. I found no figure.
How long OMCCR takes to respond after the form is submitted. The page says only "as soon as we can."
Whether reports are published, even in aggregate.
How the Poison Center and OMCCR share information, if they do.
What the April 2023 investigation found, or whether it is connected to any other event.
Whether any rule or law requires a patient to report an adverse event. I found none.
The science of how reporting systems find safety signals. That belongs to a companion piece on the science side.
Anything that has happened since October 11, 2026.

r: This article is education, not legal or medical advice. For your own situation, ask a Hawaii attorney, and for your health, ask your clinician or call the Poison Center.
