posts.title: A Public Lab for Patients
posts.subtitle: Hawaii's law promises patients direct access to certified cannabis testing. One certified lab serves the whole state. The Department of Health asked for a state reference laboratory, and the Legislature's worksheet shows $500,000 for it. Here is what the record shows, and the case for paying for patients' tests.
posts.description: Hawaii promises patients direct access to certified cannabis testing; one lab serves the state. What the reference laboratory budget request shows, and the case for subsidized home-grow tests. Education and argument, not legal advice.

r: Hawaii's dispensary law tells the Department of Health that its testing rules must include "permission for qualifying patients and primary caregivers to obtain testing services directly from certified laboratories on the island where the qualifying patient and primary caregiver reside."
That promise is in the statute. The practical question is who can use it. The Department of Health's list of certified cannabis testing facilities names one lab.

The people who most need an independent test of what they grow at home are the ones with no dispensary label to read. This article follows the promise from the statute to the budget, then argues for one use of public money: paying for patients' home-grow tests.

It is education and argument, not legal advice. Every source was opened on October 11, 2026. None comes from a conversation with an official, a lab or a patient. The argument in the last third is mine and is labeled as mine.

Section 329D-8 of the Hawaii Revised Statutes tells the Department to set testing standards, to consider "the impact of the standards on the retail cost of the product to the qualifying patient," and to include permission for patients and primary caregivers to get testing services directly from certified labs on their island.

A separate section describes how a patient or caregiver may carry a sample. Section 329-122 lets a qualifying patient or primary caregiver transport a small, capped amount of cannabis to a certified lab for testing, provided the person has secured an appointment, has a confirmation that gives the date and time and a description of the product and amount, and has the confirmation with them in transit.
A dispensary may not dispense cannabis unless a Department-certified lab has analyzed a representative sample.
The Department's registry page of certified cannabis testing facilities lists Spectra Analytical Lab, and no other.
The Department's July 2024 newsletter called it "currently the only DOH-certified cannabis testing lab in the state."

Its own site says it is certified to test for licensed dispensaries and for 329 cardholders, that it sits in Honolulu, that a person on Oahu can arrange a sample drop-off, and that full compliance samples from 329 cardholders are processed within 3 to 5 business days.

The Department's December 2024 newsletter points home growers to it: patients "have access to Spectra testing lab, which can provide a comprehensive and accurate potency result." The same passage names at-home potency test kits as "a less accurate but cost effective option."
I found no price for a patient's test in the documents I opened.

The August 2026 program data report puts the registry at 29,315 valid in-state registrations on August 31, 2026. By county of residence it lists 14,545 patients in Honolulu County, 8,153 in Hawaii County, 4,950 in Maui County and 1,568 in Kauai County, plus 99 with an out-of-state or unknown address.
So 14,671 patients, 50.05 percent, live in the three counties other than Honolulu.

Now read the interisland paragraph of section 329-122. For interisland travel, it allows transport of cannabis only between dispensaries and between a dispensary's production center or retail location and a certified lab, for testing only. It then says allowable transport "does not include interisland transportation by any means or for any purpose between a qualifying patient, primary caregiver ... and any other entity or individual."

Put those facts together. The statute promises patients testing on their own island. The one certified lab I can find is in Honolulu. The statute does not authorize a patient to carry a sample between islands. The record I opened does not say whether any lab other than the Honolulu lab takes patient samples elsewhere, or how a patient on another island is meant to use the promise. That is a gap in the record. The pieces do not obviously fit, and I make no claim that the law is broken.

In its Fiscal Year 2027 supplemental budget briefing, posted in the House Finance Committee's 2026 files, the Department of Health listed item HC-72, for program HTH 596, as a special fund request of $2,100,000 to "establish a state reference laboratory for medical cannabis and hemp."

A second page of the briefing says what the lab would do. It would "facilitate quality assurance and enforcement." Testing would cover potency, contaminant limits, certificates of analysis and labeling accuracy. The lab would support oversight of the private lab, "of which there is currently only one in Hawaiʻi." Testing "may be offered on a fee-for-service basis to external entities, particularly if the sole commercial lab operations are disrupted." The briefing calls it "a partnership with the UH College of Pharmacy" and describes the request as an increase to the special fund's spending ceiling.
Patients are not mentioned on either page.

The Legislature's final budget worksheet, dated May 20, 2026, shows the same item. On the Governor's side the detail reads "reference library," $2,100,000 for fiscal year 2027. On the conference draft side it reads "Legislature does not concur," with $500,000 in the same category, again labeled "reference library."
The enacted bill, House Bill 1800 House Draft 1, Senate Draft 1, Conference Draft 1, became Act 175 of 2026 when the governor signed it on June 26, 2026.
In Act 175's program appropriations for HTH 596, the special fund line for fiscal year 2026-27 changes from $2,425,368 to $2,925,368, a difference of $500,000.

Three cautions. The Act prints amounts, not purposes. The purpose label comes from the Legislature's own worksheet, and the Department's word for the item is "laboratory." I treat the documents as describing one request because the program, the item number and the dollar figure match, and that is my inference. Second, the size: the Department asked for $2.1 million and the worksheet shows $500,000. Third, a special fund ceiling is permission to spend what the fund collects. It is not a new source of money, and the fund is built from fees, as the section on the fund below explains.

The statute already contemplates a university role. Section 304A-1865 says the University of Hawaii may establish medical cannabis testing and research programs, subject to Department certification, that provide services to state-approved dispensaries, including assessing cannabinoid content and purity, and may charge fees.
The section came from Act 230 of 2016.
The Department's briefing names "the UH College of Pharmacy" as the partner.

The University of Hawaii at Hilo shows up in one place in my sources. The faculty page of a professor in the Daniel K. Inouye College of Pharmacy at UH Hilo lists, under current funding, "HDOH, Cannabis Analysis, PI, 08/01/2026 - 07/31/2031."

The page does not say what the work is. No document I opened names UH Hilo as the reference laboratory's host, or says the funding is the same money as the line in Act 175. The dates sit close together: Act 175 was signed on June 26, 2026, and the listed funding begins on August 1, 2026. The match looks likely to me. It is not confirmed.

blocks.x: Who can apply to be a lab

r: For comparison, the Department's testing facility application, posted in August 2026, gives the standard for any new lab. The applicant picks the areas it wants to be certified for, including potency, heavy metals, pesticides, solvents, water activity, mycotoxins and microbiology. It must be ISO 17025 accredited, have a parent company that is, or have applied, which the form calls the minimum requirement.

blocks.x: The case for paying for patients' tests

r: Everything above is record. What follows is argument.
The law has already made the promise.
Section 329D-8 asks for patient access to testing, and for the cost to patients to be weighed. A promise of access that cost or distance can block is a thin one.
Home growers are the ones without a label.

A dispensary product comes with a certificate of analysis. A patient's own harvest comes with whatever the patient can arrange. Act 46's findings say up to 45 percent of patients get cannabis from sources other than a licensed dispensary, including growing.
That is the Act's reading of a 2022 survey, and I did not verify it.
Half the patients live where there is no lab I can find.
The county table makes this concrete. Cost matters, and so does the plane ticket the statute does not let them use with a sample.
The state has a fund, and the lab it asked for can sell testing.

The medical cannabis registry and regulation special fund is built from patient registration fees and dispensary application fees, and the director of health spends it on a list of purposes, ending with "any other expenditure necessary, consistent with" the chapters.

Patient testing is not named on that list, and I do not know whether it fits. That is a question for the Department and its attorneys. The Department's own description of the reference lab includes fee-for-service testing for outside entities, which is a door a patient program could use.
A subsidy has to be designed.

My proposal is narrow. Pay the lab fee, up to a set number of tests a year, for registered patients and caregivers, by voucher, so no cash changes hands. Put a sample drop-off on each island, run by a certified lab, so no sample has to cross water. Publish aggregate results by county, with no names, so the program shows what home-grown cannabis contains. The reference lab as the Department describes it is a regulator's tool, and this would add a patient-facing service to it. Whether the law allows any of this is for a Hawaii attorney.

A published price that is already low. A drop-off on every island that I did not find. A lawful route for a patient's sample to reach a lab on another island that I did not find. Any of those would weaken the case.

blocks.x: Questions to ask before anyone builds this

items: Who pays the lab, and from which fund?
Which patients qualify, and how is that checked without exposing registry records?
How does a sample from Kauai, Maui or Hawaii island reach a lab lawfully?
Who sees the results, and are they tied to a name?
If a result shows contamination, who tells the patient, and what does the patient do next?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: What a patient's test costs, or what any lab charges.
How many registered patients grow their own cannabis, or how many have a test done.
Whether any lab other than the Honolulu lab accepts patient samples on another island.
Whether the $500,000 in Act 175 is meant to start a reference laboratory, and where it would be.
Whether UH Hilo will host one. The only link I found is a faculty funding line, and the Department's own phrase, "the UH College of Pharmacy."
Whether the reference lab would test patients' samples at all. The briefing describes regulatory uses and fee-for-service testing for outside entities.
Whether the Department asked again for the remaining $1.6 million.
Whether the special fund may be used to pay for patients' tests.
Anything that has happened since October 11, 2026.
